answers.question: What are the stages of a CI/CD pipeline (source → build → test → package → scan → deploy → verify), and what is the difference between Continuous Integration, Continuous Delivery, and Continuous Deployment?
answers.shortTitle: CI/CD Pipeline Stages and the Difference Between Continuous Integration, Delivery and Deployment

s1_definition.profdef: A CI/CD pipeline is an automated sequence of stages that takes a code change from a developer's commit all the way to a running environment. The typical stages are source (fetch the commit), build (compile and assemble artifacts), test (run unit and integration tests), package (produce a deployable artifact such as a JAR or container image), scan (static analysis and vulnerability scanning), deploy (push to an environment), and verify (smoke tests and health checks). Continuous Integration is the practice of merging and automatically building and testing every change frequently. Continuous Delivery extends CI so that every passing build is automatically prepared and ready for release, but the final push to production is a manual approval. Continuous Deployment goes one step further and releases every passing build to production automatically with no human gate.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India's cheque clearing line. A cheque (a code change) arrives at the counter (source). It is first read and stamped (build), then verified against the signature and balance (test), then put into a sealed clearing envelope (package), then checked for forgery and fraud (scan), then sent to the destination branch (deploy), and finally the destination branch confirms it landed correctly (verify). Continuous Integration is Rajesh and Priya both dropping their cheques into the same clearing line many times a day and the machine immediately checking each one. Continuous Delivery means every verified cheque is packed and sitting ready at the vault door, but a manager must press the button to release it. Continuous Deployment means the machine releases it automatically with no manager needed.
s1_definition.oneliner: CI proves the code is good, Continuous Delivery keeps it release-ready behind a button, and Continuous Deployment presses that button automatically.

sections.s2_technical:
The source stage is where the pipeline begins. A trigger such as a Git push or a merged pull request causes the CI server to check out the exact commit. For example, a Jenkins pipeline step `checkout scm` or a GitHub Actions step `uses: actions/checkout@v4` pulls the banking service source at a known SHA so every later stage works on identical code.

The build stage compiles the source and assembles the primary artifact. For a Spring Boot banking service this is usually `mvn clean package -DskipTests` which produces a runnable JAR. Separating build from test lets you fail fast on compilation errors before spending time running tests.

The test stage runs automated tests. Unit tests run first because they are fast, for example `mvn test` running a `TransferServiceTest` that checks a debit and credit leave balances correct. Integration tests run next, often against a throwaway database spun up with Testcontainers, so a `TransferControllerIT` can verify the real HTTP endpoint and the real SQL. A failing test here stops the pipeline so broken code never reaches an environment.

The package stage turns the tested code into a deployable unit. In a container world this is building an image, for example `docker build -t registry.bank.local/transfer-service:1.4.2 .` and tagging it with the build number so the exact artifact is traceable.

The scan stage enforces quality and security. Static analysis with SonarQube checks code smells and coverage and can fail the build if a quality gate is breached. Vulnerability scanning with Trivy checks the image layers and dependencies, for example `trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL registry.bank.local/transfer-service:1.4.2`, which fails the pipeline if a critical CVE is present in a library the banking service pulls in.

The deploy stage pushes the artifact to an environment. This might be `kubectl set image deployment/transfer-service transfer-service=registry.bank.local/transfer-service:1.4.2` for a Kubernetes rollout, or a Helm upgrade. In a mature setup deployment is split per environment: dev first, then QA, then production.

The verify stage confirms the deployment is actually healthy. A smoke test calls the live health endpoint, for example `curl -f https://transfer.bank.local/actuator/health`, and a few business smoke checks confirm a test transfer succeeds. If verify fails, the pipeline rolls back.

The three terms differ by how far automation reaches. Continuous Integration stops at a green build and test. Continuous Delivery automates everything up to a production-ready artifact but keeps a manual approval before production, which is common in banking because a human must sign off before touching the live ledger. Continuous Deployment removes even that gate, so every green build reaches customers automatically. A senior nuance is that regulated banking systems almost always use Continuous Delivery to production with an approval, while using full Continuous Deployment freely for lower environments like dev and QA.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, Rajesh commits a change to the transfer service that accidentally breaks the fee calculation. In the old days nobody noticed until a tester manually ran the app days later, by which time three more changes had piled on top and it was impossible to tell which commit broke it. This is exactly the problem Continuous Integration solves. Every commit is built and tested automatically within minutes, so the moment Rajesh's bad fee logic lands, the pipeline fails and points straight at his commit.

Problem 2 — Even when the code is good, the team used to deploy by hand, copying JARs onto servers at midnight. One engineer deployed the wrong version to production and a day of transfers used stale fee tables. This is exactly the problem a packaging and deploy pipeline solves. The pipeline builds one immutable artifact, tags it with the commit, and that exact artifact is what gets promoted through dev, QA, and production, so there is never a mismatch.

Problem 3 — A security audit found that a vulnerable logging library had been running in production for months. Nobody scanned artifacts before release. This is exactly the problem the scan stage solves. Every image is scanned for known vulnerabilities and the build fails if a critical issue is present, so vulnerable code is blocked before it ever reaches the banking environment.

To make this concrete without a real Jenkins server, we will write a small Java program that simulates a CI/CD pipeline. We will model each stage as a class implementing a common `PipelineStage` interface. We will have a `SourceStage`, `BuildStage`, `TestStage`, `PackageStage`, `ScanStage`, `DeployStage`, and `VerifyStage`. A `Pipeline` orchestrator runs them in order, stops on the first failure, and prints a clear report. We will run it once for a healthy commit that passes all stages and once for a commit with a failing test so you can see the pipeline stop early. This mirrors the real behaviour where a red stage halts promotion to the next environment.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a Git commit identified by a SHA. We run two: the healthy commit `a1b2c3-healthy` and the broken commit `x9y8z7-bad-test`.

Step 1: For the healthy commit, the SourceStage receives the SHA, confirms it is non-blank, and returns success with the message that it checked out the commit. The data at this point is just the identifier of the change.

Step 2: The BuildStage runs and reports that it compiled the transfer service and produced the JAR. Nothing about the commit identifier changes; we are now holding a built artifact conceptually.

Step 3: The TestStage inspects the commit identifier. Because it does not contain the marker `bad-test`, it returns success with 42 tests passing and 86% coverage. The gate stays green.

Step 4: The PackageStage builds an image tag by appending the SHA to the registry path, producing `registry.bank.local/transfer-service:a1b2c3-healthy`. The artifact is now immutable and traceable to the commit.

Step 5: The ScanStage checks for the marker `cve`, does not find it, and returns success with the quality gate passed and Trivy clean.

Step 6: The DeployStage reports the image rolled out to dev. Step 7: the VerifyStage reports the health check up and a smoke transfer from SAV2001 to CUR3001 succeeded. The pipeline prints overall success and promotes the artifact.

Step 8: For the broken commit, stages one and two pass, but at the TestStage the identifier contains `bad-test`, so it returns failure. The orchestrator logs the failure and immediately halts, so the package, scan, deploy, and verify stages never run and nothing broken reaches an environment.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A CI/CD pipeline is an automated sequence that carries a code change from commit to a running environment through well-defined stages: source checks out the exact commit, build compiles and assembles the artifact, test runs unit and integration tests, package produces an immutable deployable such as a container image tagged with the commit, scan runs static analysis and vulnerability checks with quality gates, deploy pushes to an environment, and verify confirms health with smoke tests. The key design principle is fail fast and promote only what is proven, so a red stage immediately halts promotion and nothing broken moves forward.

The three terms are often confused, so I keep them precise. Continuous Integration is the discipline of merging every change frequently and automatically building and testing it, which catches integration problems within minutes rather than days. Continuous Delivery extends that so every passing build is automatically prepared as a release-ready artifact, but the final push to production stays behind a manual approval. Continuous Deployment removes even that gate and releases every green build straight to production automatically.

In banking the distinction matters a lot. At the National Bank of India we ran full Continuous Deployment in the dev and QA environments because speed there is pure upside, but production used Continuous Delivery with a human approval gate, because a regulator and an auditor expect a named person to sign off before the live ledger changes. That approval was not a bottleneck because everything before it was automated and the artifact was already proven.

On the project I built a pipeline for the transfer service where every commit was built, tested against a Testcontainers Postgres, scanned with SonarQube for a coverage and quality gate, and scanned with Trivy for critical CVEs, and only then packaged into an image tagged with the commit SHA. That tagged image was the single artifact promoted through every environment, which eliminated the classic problem of deploying the wrong version. The senior point I always add is that the artifact must be immutable and traceable to a commit, and that verify is not optional — a deploy that is not confirmed healthy is treated as a failure and rolled back automatically.

answers.question: How do you separate CI and CD pipelines in Jenkins (triggers at each stage), and how is Jenkins integrated with a Kubernetes cluster (agents as pods, Kubernetes plugin)?
answers.shortTitle: Separating CI and CD Pipelines in Jenkins and Integrating Jenkins with Kubernetes

s1_definition.profdef: In Jenkins, separating CI from CD means running two distinct pipelines with different triggers: a CI pipeline triggered automatically on every push or pull request that builds, tests, scans, and publishes an immutable artifact, and a CD pipeline triggered by the successful completion of CI (or by a tag, or by a manual promotion) that takes that already-built artifact and deploys it to an environment. Jenkins integrates with Kubernetes through the Kubernetes plugin, which runs build agents as ephemeral pods inside the cluster: when a job starts, Jenkins asks the Kubernetes API to create a pod with the required tool containers, the build runs inside that pod, and the pod is destroyed afterward, giving clean, isolated, horizontally scalable build capacity.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India having two separate assembly lines. The first line (CI) takes raw cheque forms, checks them, and seals them into certified envelopes — it runs automatically every time a form arrives. The second line (CD) takes only certified envelopes and delivers them to the right branch — it only starts when the first line hands over a certified envelope, and for the main vault it waits for a manager's signature. For staffing, instead of keeping a hall full of permanent clerks sitting idle, the bank hires temporary clerks on demand: each cheque batch gets its own clerk who appears, does the work, and leaves. In Jenkins-on-Kubernetes terms, each build gets its own pod that spins up, runs the job, and disappears.
s1_definition.oneliner: CI builds and certifies an artifact on every push, CD deploys that same artifact when CI passes, and Jenkins runs each build in a throwaway Kubernetes pod.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In Jenkins, separating CI from CD means running two distinct pipelines with different triggers: a CI pipeline triggered automatically on every push or pull request that builds, tests, scans, and publishes an immutable artifact, and a CD pipeline triggered by the successful completion of CI (or by a tag, or by a manual promotion) that takes that already-built artifact and deploys it to an environment. Jenkins integrates with Kubernetes through the Kubernetes plugin, which runs build agents as ephemeral pods inside the cluster: when a job starts, Jenkins asks the Kubernetes API to create a pod with the required tool containers, the build runs inside that pod, and the pod is destroyed afterward, giving clean, isolated, horizontally scalable build capacity.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the National Bank of India having two separate assembly lines. The first line (CI) takes raw cheque forms, checks them, and seals them into certified envelopes — it runs automatically every time a form arrives. The second line (CD) takes only certified envelopes and delivers them to the right branch — it only starts when the first line hands over a certified envelope, and for the main vault it waits for a manager's signature. For staffing, instead of keeping a hall full of permanent clerks sitting idle, the bank hires temporary clerks on demand: each cheque batch gets its own clerk who appears, does the work, and leaves. In Jenkins-on-Kubernetes terms, each build gets its own pod that spins up, runs the job, and disappears.

**One line to remember:** CI builds and certifies an artifact on every push, CD deploys that same artifact when CI passes, and Jenkins runs each build in a throwaway Kubernetes pod.

sections.s2_technical:
Separating the two pipelines starts with triggers. The CI pipeline is defined in a `Jenkinsfile` and triggered by a source event. With the GitHub or GitLab plugin this is a webhook on push and pull request, configured with `triggers { githubPush() }` or by the multibranch pipeline scanning branches. Its job is to build, run tests, scan, and on success publish an artifact to a registry or repository manager, tagged with the commit. It must never deploy to an environment; its only output is a trustworthy artifact.

The CD pipeline is a separate job triggered by the CI result. A common way is the `build` step: at the end of CI you call `build job: 'transfer-service-cd', parameters: [string(name: 'IMAGE_TAG', value: env.GIT_COMMIT)]`, passing the exact artifact tag forward. Alternatively CD is triggered by a Git tag push for releases, or started manually by an operator who picks which already-built artifact to promote. Because CD receives a tag and never rebuilds, the thing tested in CI is exactly the thing deployed.

Environment promotion lives inside the CD pipeline as ordered stages with gates. A typical flow deploys to dev automatically, then to QA automatically, then pauses with an `input` step for human approval before production: `stage('Prod') { steps { input message: 'Deploy to production?', submitter: 'release-managers' }; ... }`. The `submitter` restricts who may approve, which in banking maps to a named release manager.

The Kubernetes integration is configured through the Kubernetes plugin on the Jenkins controller. You point Jenkins at the cluster API server and a namespace, and define a pod template. When a pipeline requests an agent with that label, Jenkins calls the Kubernetes API to create a pod. The pod usually has several containers: a JNLP container that talks back to the Jenkins controller, plus tool containers such as a Maven container to build and a Docker or Kaniko container to build images. The declarative syntax uses a `kubernetes` agent with a YAML pod spec.

Running agents as pods gives three big benefits. First, isolation: each build runs in a fresh pod with no leftover state from a previous build, which prevents one banking service's build from contaminating another. Second, elastic scale: if ten pull requests land at once, Jenkins asks Kubernetes for ten pods and they run in parallel, then the pods are destroyed, so you are not paying for idle agents. Third, consistency: the pod template pins exact tool versions, so every build uses the same Maven and JDK, removing the classic "works on my agent" problem.

A senior nuance is image building inside a pod. Mounting the host Docker socket is a security risk on a shared banking cluster because it gives the build root-equivalent access to the node. The safer pattern is Kaniko or Buildah, which build images in userspace without a Docker daemon, so a compromised build cannot take over the node. Another nuance is credentials: CD needs cluster deploy credentials and registry credentials, and these must come from Jenkins credential store or a secret manager injected at runtime, never baked into the Jenkinsfile.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India the team originally had one giant pipeline that built and deployed in a single run. When Priya just wanted to redeploy a known-good build to QA, she had to rebuild from scratch, which took twenty minutes and risked producing a slightly different artifact if a dependency had moved. This is exactly the problem CI/CD separation solves. CI produces one immutable artifact once; CD simply promotes that existing artifact, so redeploying is fast and byte-for-byte identical.

Problem 2 — The old pipeline ran on two permanent build servers. During a busy release day, ten merges queued up behind each other because only two builds could run at once, and the next morning those same servers sat idle wasting money. This is exactly the problem Jenkins-on-Kubernetes solves. Each build gets its own pod on demand, ten builds run in parallel across the cluster, and when the rush is over the pods vanish so nothing sits idle.

Problem 3 — A production incident happened when someone deployed straight to the live ledger with no approval. This is exactly the problem a CD approval gate solves. The CD pipeline deploys to dev and QA automatically, but pauses at an input step before production that only a named release manager can approve.

To make this concrete without a live Jenkins cluster, we will write a small Java simulation. We will model a `CiPipeline` that produces an immutable `Artifact` (an image tag) on a push event, and a `CdPipeline` that consumes an `Artifact` and promotes it through dev, QA, and production, pausing for approval before production. We will model build capacity with an `AgentPool` that represents Kubernetes pods created on demand and released after use. We will run a healthy push that builds an artifact and promotes it, showing the approval gate holding production until a release manager approves. This mirrors the real two-pipeline, pod-per-build design.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a push of commit `a1b2c3d4` for the transfer service, plus two attempts to promote the resulting artifact to production, one by an unauthorised developer and one by an authorised release manager.

Step 1: The push triggers CI. The AgentPool creates a pod `jenkins-agent-ci-1`, representing Jenkins asking Kubernetes for a build pod. The data is still just a commit identifier.

Step 2: Inside that pod, CI compiles, runs tests, and scans. It then constructs an immutable Artifact whose image tag is `registry.bank.local/transfer-service:a1b2c3d4`. The commit has now become a concrete, tagged artifact.

Step 3: CI finishes and the pod is released, representing Kubernetes destroying the build pod so nothing sits idle. The artifact survives because it was published to the registry.

Step 4: CD starts for the first promotion attempt. A new pod `jenkins-agent-cd-1` is created. CD deploys the same artifact to dev and QA automatically, changing the deployed image in those namespaces while the artifact itself stays identical.

Step 5: CD reaches the production approval gate. The approver is `rajesh-dev`, who is not in the release managers set, so the gate denies approval. Production is not touched and CD returns failure. The pod is released.

Step 6: CD starts again for the second attempt with approver `priya-release-mgr`. It redeploys the same artifact to dev and QA, reaches the gate, and this time the approver is authorised, so the gate approves and CD deploys the identical artifact to production.

sections.s6_takeaway:
In Jenkins I keep continuous integration and continuous delivery as two separate pipelines with different triggers. The CI pipeline is triggered automatically by a push or pull request webhook. Its only responsibility is to build, run unit and integration tests, run static analysis and vulnerability scans, and on success publish a single immutable artifact, usually a container image tagged with the commit SHA, to a registry. It must never deploy to an environment. The CD pipeline is triggered by CI success, typically with a post-success build step that passes the image tag forward, or by a release tag. Its only responsibility is to take that already-built artifact and promote it, so what was tested is exactly what is deployed, and redeploying to any environment is fast and byte-for-byte identical.

Inside the CD pipeline I model environment promotion as ordered stages with gates. Dev and QA deploy automatically, and production sits behind an input approval step restricted by submitter to named release managers. In banking that gate is essential, because a regulator expects a specific person to authorise any change to the live ledger, and the submitter restriction means only a release manager, not any developer, can approve.

For build capacity I integrate Jenkins with Kubernetes using the Kubernetes plugin. Instead of permanent build servers, each job requests an ephemeral agent pod. Jenkins calls the Kubernetes API, a pod is created with the exact tool containers it needs such as Maven and Kaniko, the build runs inside that pod, and the pod is destroyed afterward. This gives clean isolation so builds never contaminate each other, elastic parallelism so a rush of ten merges simply spins up ten pods, and pinned tool versions so there is no "works on my agent" drift.

On the banking project I ran exactly this setup for the transfer service. CI built and published an image tagged with the commit, CD promoted that image through dev, QA, and production with a release-manager approval before production, and every build ran in a throwaway pod. The senior point I always add is that I use Kaniko rather than mounting the host Docker socket, because mounting the socket on a shared cluster gives a build node-level root access, which is unacceptable for a system handling real money. Credentials for the cluster and registry come from the Jenkins credential store or Vault and are injected at runtime, never written into the Jenkinsfile.

---

answers.question: What is a Jenkins Scripted vs Declarative pipeline, and what is Groovy's role in a `Jenkinsfile`?
answers.shortTitle: Jenkins Scripted vs Declarative Pipeline and Groovy's Role in a Jenkinsfile

s1_definition.profdef: A `Jenkinsfile` defines a pipeline as code and can be written in two styles. A Declarative pipeline uses a structured, opinionated syntax wrapped in a top-level `pipeline { }` block with predefined sections like `agent`, `stages`, `steps`, `environment`, `post`, and built-in constructs for conditions and approvals; it is easier to read and validate. A Scripted pipeline is written as a Groovy program inside a `node { }` block with full imperative control such as loops, variables, functions, and try/catch; it is more flexible but more error-prone. Both are executed by the Jenkins Groovy engine, so Groovy is the underlying language in both cases: Declarative is a Groovy-based domain-specific language with guardrails, while Scripted is closer to raw Groovy.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of two ways to write the National Bank of India's cheque-processing procedure. The Declarative way is a standard printed form with fixed boxes: "Branch:", "Steps:", "Approval:", "On failure:". Anyone can fill it in correctly and a supervisor can glance at it and immediately see if a box is missing. The Scripted way is a blank notebook where you write the whole procedure freehand in full sentences, with if-this-then-that logic and loops; it can express anything, but it is easier to make a mistake and harder for a supervisor to check. Both notebooks and forms are ultimately read by the same clerk (the Groovy engine) who carries out the instructions.
s1_definition.oneliner: Declarative is a structured Groovy DSL with guardrails for readability, Scripted is free-form Groovy for maximum flexibility, and Groovy is the engine running both.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A `Jenkinsfile` defines a pipeline as code and can be written in two styles. A Declarative pipeline uses a structured, opinionated syntax wrapped in a top-level `pipeline { }` block with predefined sections like `agent`, `stages`, `steps`, `environment`, `post`, and built-in constructs for conditions and approvals; it is easier to read and validate. A Scripted pipeline is written as a Groovy program inside a `node { }` block with full imperative control such as loops, variables, functions, and try/catch; it is more flexible but more error-prone. Both are executed by the Jenkins Groovy engine, so Groovy is the underlying language in both cases: Declarative is a Groovy-based domain-specific language with guardrails, while Scripted is closer to raw Groovy.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of two ways to write the National Bank of India's cheque-processing procedure. The Declarative way is a standard printed form with fixed boxes: "Branch:", "Steps:", "Approval:", "On failure:". Anyone can fill it in correctly and a supervisor can glance at it and immediately see if a box is missing. The Scripted way is a blank notebook where you write the whole procedure freehand in full sentences, with if-this-then-that logic and loops; it can express anything, but it is easier to make a mistake and harder for a supervisor to check. Both notebooks and forms are ultimately read by the same clerk (the Groovy engine) who carries out the instructions.

**One line to remember:** Declarative is a structured Groovy DSL with guardrails for readability, Scripted is free-form Groovy for maximum flexibility, and Groovy is the engine running both.

sections.s2_technical:
A Declarative pipeline always starts with `pipeline { }` at the top level. Inside it you declare an `agent` (where it runs), an `environment` block for variables, a `stages` block containing named `stage` blocks, and each stage has a `steps` block with the actual commands. For example a stage looks like `stage('Build') { steps { sh 'mvn clean package' } }`. Declarative gives you built-in sections such as `post { always { } success { } failure { } }` for cleanup and notifications, `when { branch 'main' }` for conditional execution, `input` for approvals, and `options` for things like timeouts. Jenkins validates the structure up front, so a malformed Declarative pipeline is rejected before it runs.

A Scripted pipeline starts with `node { }` and is essentially a Groovy script. You write imperative code directly: assign variables, use `if` and `for`, define functions, and call steps like `stage('Build') { sh 'mvn clean package' }`. Because it is a real program you can do things like loop over a list of microservices and build each, or compute a deployment target from arbitrary logic. The cost is that there are fewer guardrails; a typo or a logic bug surfaces at runtime, and the structure is harder for a reviewer to scan.

Groovy is central to both. Jenkins pipelines run on a Groovy interpreter (specifically a sandboxed, continuation-passing variant called CPS so pipelines can survive a controller restart). In a Declarative pipeline, Groovy still appears inside a `script { }` block when you need real logic, for example `script { def tag = sh(returnStdout: true, script: 'git rev-parse HEAD').trim() }`. In a Scripted pipeline the whole file is Groovy. Understanding Groovy matters because you use its string interpolation, collections, closures, and the `sh`, `echo`, and `error` steps that Jenkins exposes.

Shared Libraries bring the two worlds together. Reusable logic is written as Groovy in a versioned repository and called from either style, for example `bankDeploy(service: 'transfer-service', env: 'qa')`. This keeps the per-service `Jenkinsfile` tiny while the complex Groovy lives in one audited place.

A senior nuance is when to choose each. The strong default in a regulated banking environment is Declarative, because its structure is easy to read, review, and validate, and the standard sections cover almost everything. You drop into a `script { }` block or a Shared Library for the rare bits of real logic. Pure Scripted is reserved for genuinely dynamic needs, such as generating stages at runtime for an unknown number of services, and even then the logic is usually pushed into a Shared Library so the pipeline file stays clean. Another nuance is the CPS sandbox: not all Groovy is allowed, certain methods are blocked for security, and heavy in-pipeline Groovy computation is discouraged because it runs on the controller, not the agent.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, Rajesh wrote the first pipeline as a free-form Scripted file with lots of if-else logic to decide which environment to deploy to. It worked, but when Priya tried to review it before an audit she could not quickly tell what the stages were or what happened on failure, because it was buried in Groovy logic. This is exactly the problem the Declarative style solves. Declarative forces a clear structure with named stages and a post block, so a reviewer sees the shape of the pipeline instantly.

Problem 2 — The team had twelve microservices and each copy-pasted the same forty lines of deploy logic. When they needed to add a vulnerability scan, they had to edit twelve files and missed two. This is exactly the problem Groovy Shared Libraries solve. The deploy logic lives once as Groovy in a versioned library, and each service calls a single step, so a change is made in one audited place.

Problem 3 — Occasionally the team genuinely needed dynamic behaviour, such as building a variable list of services discovered at runtime. Pure Declarative could not express that cleanly. This is exactly where a Groovy `script { }` block or Scripted logic earns its place, kept small and ideally inside the library.

To make this concrete without a Jenkins server we will write a small Java simulation that contrasts the two styles. We will model a `DeclarativePipeline` as a fixed, ordered structure of named stages with a post-action, and a `ScriptedPipeline` as a class that builds its stages with arbitrary imperative logic (a loop over services). We will also model a `SharedLibrary` step `bankDeploy` that both styles call, proving reuse. We will run a Declarative pipeline for the transfer service and a Scripted pipeline that dynamically builds a deploy stage per service, so you can see the structured versus free-form difference side by side.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A `Jenkinsfile` defines a pipeline as code, and there are two styles. A Declarative pipeline uses a structured, opinionated syntax inside a top-level `pipeline` block with fixed sections such as agent, environment, stages, steps, and post. It is easy to read, easy to review, and Jenkins validates its structure before it runs, so a malformed pipeline is rejected early. A Scripted pipeline is written inside a `node` block as a full Groovy program with variables, loops, conditionals, and functions. It is far more flexible but has fewer guardrails, so mistakes surface at runtime and reviewers find it harder to follow.

Groovy is the common foundation. Both styles run on the Jenkins Groovy engine, specifically a sandboxed continuation-passing variant so a pipeline can survive a controller restart. In a Declarative pipeline you still drop into a `script` block of real Groovy when you need genuine logic, while a Scripted pipeline is Groovy from top to bottom. Knowing Groovy matters because you rely on its string interpolation, collections, and closures, and on the steps Jenkins exposes like sh, echo, and error.

My default in a regulated banking environment is Declarative, because audit and review are first-class concerns and the structured form makes the stages, conditions, and failure handling obvious at a glance. I reserve Scripted for genuinely dynamic needs, such as generating a variable number of deploy stages for a list of services discovered at runtime, and even then I push the heavy logic into a Groovy Shared Library so the pipeline file stays small and the complex code lives in one versioned, audited place.

On the banking project the transfer service used a clean Declarative pipeline with Build, Test, and a Deploy stage gated by branch, a post block that always archived artifacts and published test reports, and a failure handler that alerted the channel. The actual deploy logic was a single shared library step, bankDeploy, that every one of our twelve services called, so when we added a vulnerability scan we changed one library file instead of twelve pipelines. The senior point I always add is that I avoid heavy Groovy computation directly in the pipeline because it runs on the controller rather than the agent and can slow the whole instance, and that the CPS sandbox blocks certain methods for security, so library code is the right home for anything non-trivial.

answers.question: How do you avoid writing a separate pipeline for every one of thousands of microservices — Jenkins Shared Libraries (reusable Groovy steps in a versioned repo) and generic parameterized/templated pipelines (one `Jenkinsfile` + per-service config) — and how do you trigger the right environment pipeline per branch (dev→Dev, qa→QA) with approvals/gates before Prod?
answers.shortTitle: Avoiding a Separate Pipeline per Microservice — Shared Libraries, Templated Pipelines, and Per-Branch Environment Routing

s1_definition.profdef: To avoid maintaining thousands of near-identical pipelines, you centralise the pipeline logic. A Jenkins Shared Library is a versioned Groovy repository containing reusable steps and a full pipeline template, loaded with `@Library`. Each microservice then keeps only a tiny `Jenkinsfile` that calls the template and supplies per-service configuration, often from a small file like `bank-ci.yaml`. Environment routing is driven by the branch name: the template maps the current branch to a target environment (for example `dev` branch to the Dev namespace, `qa` branch to QA) and inserts an approval gate before Prod. This gives one place to change CI behaviour for every service at once, while each service controls only what is genuinely unique to it.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has thousands of branches, and nobody writes a separate operations manual for each one. Instead there is one master manual kept at head office (the Shared Library), and every branch just has a one-page cover sheet saying "we are branch SAV2001, our manager is Priya, follow the master manual." When head office improves a procedure, every branch gets it immediately. s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** To avoid maintaining thousands of near-identical pipelines, you centralise the pipeline logic. A Jenkins Shared Library is a versioned Groovy repository containing reusable steps and a full pipeline template, loaded with `@Library`. Each microservice then keeps only a tiny `Jenkinsfile` that calls the template and supplies per-service configuration, often from a small file like `bank-ci.yaml`. Environment routing is driven by the branch name: the template maps the current branch to a target environment (for example `dev` branch to the Dev namespace, `qa` branch to QA) and inserts an approval gate before Prod. This gives one place to change CI behaviour for every service at once, while each service controls only what is genuinely unique to it.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has thousands of branches, and nobody writes a separate operations manual for each one. Instead there is one master manual kept at head office (the Shared Library), and every branch just has a one-page cover sheet saying "we are branch SAV2001, our manager is Priya, follow the master manual." When head office improves a procedure, every branch gets it immediately. Which counter a cheque goes to depends on which door it came through: the "dev" door routes to the practice counter, the "qa" door to the testing counter, and the main vault always needs a manager's signature. In pipeline terms, the branch name is the door, and the master manual routes the work and enforces the signature before production.

**One line to remember:** One versioned Shared Library plus a tiny per-service config replaces thousands of copy-pasted pipelines, and the branch name decides the environment with an approval gate before Prod.

sections.s2_technical:
A Shared Library is a Git repository with a fixed layout. The `vars/` directory holds global steps, each a Groovy file whose name is the step name, so `vars/bankPipeline.groovy` becomes a callable step `bankPipeline`. The `src/` directory holds regular Groovy classes for more structured logic, for example `src/com/bank/ci/Deployer.groovy`. The library is registered in Jenkins global configuration or loaded per-job with `@Library('bank-shared-lib@v3') _`, and pinning to a tag like `v3` means every service gets a known, audited version rather than whatever is on the main branch.

The templated pipeline pattern puts the entire pipeline inside one library step, usually `bankPipeline`, which contains the standard build, test, scan, package, and deploy stages. Each microservice's `Jenkinsfile` shrinks to a few lines: `@Library('bank-shared-lib@v3') _` followed by `bankPipeline(service: 'transfer-service', javaVersion: 21, deployTargets: ['dev','qa','prod'])`. Per-service variation that cannot be a simple parameter is read from a small config file checked into the service repo, such as `bank-ci.yaml`, which the template loads with `readYaml`. This is "one Jenkinsfile logic, per-service config."

Branch-to-environment routing lives in the template. The template reads `env.BRANCH_NAME` and maps it: a push to `dev` deploys to the Dev namespace, a push to `qa` deploys to QA, and `main` or a release tag targets Prod. In Declarative you express this with `when { branch 'qa' }` on the QA deploy stage, or in the library with a Groovy map such as `def envFor = [dev:'dev-ns', qa:'qa-ns', main:'prod-ns']`. Because the mapping is in one place, every service routes consistently.

Approvals and gates guard Prod. The Prod deploy stage in the template is preceded by an `input` step restricted by `submitter` to a named group such as release managers, and often wrapped in a `timeout` so an unapproved release eventually aborts rather than hanging forever. Lower environments have no gate so they stay fast. The gate is defined once in the library, so no service can accidentally skip it.

A senior nuance is governance. Pinning the library to a version tag gives reproducibility and an audit trail, and library changes themselves go through code review and their own tests, because a bug in a shared step breaks every service at once. Another nuance is safe parameter handling: per-service config must be validated (unknown keys rejected, dangerous values sanitised) because the template runs with broad permissions. A third nuance is that truly service-specific stages are supported by letting the config declare extra steps or by the template calling an optional hook like `preDeploy` if the service defines one, so the template stays generic without blocking special cases.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India grew from five services to over two hundred, each with its own copy-pasted two-hundred-line `Jenkinsfile`. When the security team mandated a new image scan, someone had to edit two hundred files and inevitably missed several, leaving unscanned services in production. This is exactly the problem a Shared Library solves. The scan is added once to the template step and every service picks it up on the next build.

Problem 2 — Each service's pipeline hardcoded its own environment logic, and they drifted. One service deployed the `qa` branch to Dev by mistake for months. This is exactly the problem centralised branch-to-environment routing solves. The template owns the mapping from branch to namespace, so every service routes identically and correctly.

Problem 3 — A junior engineer's pipeline deployed straight to Prod with no approval because they forgot to add the gate. This is exactly the problem a template-owned approval gate solves. The Prod stage in the library always requires a release-manager approval, and no service can omit it because no service writes that stage.

To make this concrete without a Jenkins cluster we will write a Java simulation of the templated model. We will build a `BankPipelineTemplate` (the library step) that takes a `ServiceConfig` (the per-service config) and a branch name, maps the branch to an environment, runs the standard stages, and enforces an approval gate before Prod. We will model two services, `transfer-service` and `fraud-service`, each supplying only its own config, and run the template for a `qa` branch (auto-deploys to QA) and a `main` branch (requires approval before Prod). This mirrors one template serving many services with per-branch routing and a Prod gate.

The input is two services, each with only its own config, and three pipeline runs on different branches.

Step 1: The template is created once with a centralised EnvironmentRouter and a single ApprovalGate holding the authorised release managers. This is the shared logic every service will reuse.

Step 2: For the first run, the transfer service config is passed with branch `qa`. The template runs build, test, scan, and package using the service's Java version from its config. The config stays per-service; the stages come from the template.

Step 3: The router maps branch `qa` to the `qa-ns` environment. QA is not production, so no approval is needed, and the template deploys the transfer service to QA.

Step 4: For the second run, the fraud service config is passed with branch `main`. The template runs the same standard stages, then the router maps `main` to `prod-ns`.

Step 5: Because the target is production, the gate checks the approver `rajesh-dev`, who is not a release manager, so approval is denied and the deploy is blocked. Nothing reaches Prod.

Step 6: For the third run, the fraud service is deployed on branch `main` again but with approver `priya-release-mgr`, who is authorised, so the gate approves and the template deploys the fraud service to Prod. The same template served both services, routed by branch, with the Prod gate enforced centrally.

sections.s6_takeaway:
To avoid maintaining thousands of near-identical pipelines, I centralise the pipeline logic in a Jenkins Shared Library, which is a versioned Groovy repository with reusable steps under a vars directory and structured classes under src. The entire standard pipeline lives in one library step, commonly bankPipeline, containing the build, test, scan, package, and deploy stages. Each microservice then keeps a tiny Jenkinsfile that just loads the library and calls that step, passing only what is genuinely unique to it, with anything more complex coming from a small per-service config file like bank-ci.yaml. The payoff is that when the security team mandates a new image scan, I add it once to the template and every service picks it up on its next build, instead of editing hundreds of files and missing some.

Environment routing is driven by the branch name and owned entirely by the template. A push to the dev branch deploys to the Dev namespace, qa to QA, and main or a release tag to Prod. Because that mapping lives in one place, every service routes identically and no service can drift into deploying the wrong branch to the wrong environment.

Production is protected by an approval gate that the template defines once. The Prod deploy stage is preceded by an input step restricted by submitter to a named release-manager group and wrapped in a timeout, so an unapproved release eventually aborts rather than hanging. Lower environments have no gate, so they stay fast, and crucially no service can skip the Prod gate because no service writes that stage.

On the banking project this took us from over two hundred copy-pasted pipelines to one audited template plus a two-line Jenkinsfile per service. The transfer service and the fraud service both called bankPipeline with just their name and Java version, the branch decided the environment, and Prod always required Priya, our release manager, to approve. The senior point I always add is governance: the library is pinned to a version tag like v3 so every service gets a known, reproducible version, and changes to the library itself go through code review and their own tests, because a bug in a shared step would break every service at once. I also validate the per-service config and treat unknown keys as errors, because the template runs with broad permissions.

answers.question: What is GitOps (ArgoCD/Flux) — Git as the single source of truth with a controller continuously reconciling the cluster to the declared manifests (pull-based) — and how does it differ from a push-based Jenkins deploy (auditability, automatic drift correction, easy rollback via `git revert`)?
answers.shortTitle: GitOps (ArgoCD/Flux) Versus Push-Based Jenkins Deploys

s1_definition.profdef: GitOps is an operational model where a Git repository holds the complete declared desired state of a system as manifests, and a controller running inside the cluster, such as ArgoCD or Flux, continuously compares the live cluster to that Git state and reconciles any difference by pulling and applying the manifests. It is pull-based: the cluster converges itself toward Git rather than an external tool pushing changes in. A push-based Jenkins deploy is the opposite: a pipeline from outside the cluster runs commands like `kubectl apply` to imperatively push a change into the cluster. GitOps gives stronger auditability (every change is a reviewed Git commit), automatic drift correction (the controller undoes any out-of-band change), and trivial rollback (a `git revert` restores the previous declared state).
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India's official rulebook for how every branch must be set up. In GitOps, the rulebook lives in a locked, version-controlled master binder (Git), and each branch has an inspector (the controller) who constantly walks the floor comparing reality to the rulebook and silently fixing anything that drifted — a moved desk, an unauthorised sign. To change a branch, you do not touch the branch directly; you amend the master binder through a reviewed change, and the inspector makes reality match. The old push model is like head office sending a courier who physically rearranges the branch; if someone later moves a desk, nobody notices, and to undo a change you need another courier trip. GitOps makes the binder the single truth and the inspector keep reality honest.
s1_definition.oneliner: GitOps makes Git the single source of truth and an in-cluster controller continuously pulls reality toward it, so you get audit, automatic drift correction, and rollback by git revert — unlike a push-based Jenkins kubectl apply.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** GitOps is an operational model where a Git repository holds the complete declared desired state of a system as manifests, and a controller running inside the cluster, such as ArgoCD or Flux, continuously compares the live cluster to that Git state and reconciles any difference by pulling and applying the manifests. It is pull-based: the cluster converges itself toward Git rather than an external tool pushing changes in. A push-based Jenkins deploy is the opposite: a pipeline from outside the cluster runs commands like `kubectl apply` to imperatively push a change into the cluster. GitOps gives stronger auditability (every change is a reviewed Git commit), automatic drift correction (the controller undoes any out-of-band change), and trivial rollback (a `git revert` restores the previous declared state).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India's official rulebook for how every branch must be set up. In GitOps, the rulebook lives in a locked, version-controlled master binder (Git), and each branch has an inspector (the controller) who constantly walks the floor comparing reality to the rulebook and silently fixing anything that drifted — a moved desk, an unauthorised sign. To change a branch, you do not touch the branch directly; you amend the master binder through a reviewed change, and the inspector makes reality match. The old push model is like head office sending a courier who physically rearranges the branch; if someone later moves a desk, nobody notices, and to undo a change you need another courier trip. GitOps makes the binder the single truth and the inspector keep reality honest.

**One line to remember:** GitOps makes Git the single source of truth and an in-cluster controller continuously pulls reality toward it, so you get audit, automatic drift correction, and rollback by git revert — unlike a push-based Jenkins kubectl apply.

sections.s2_technical:
In GitOps the desired state is declarative and lives in Git. For a banking service this is a set of Kubernetes manifests, usually Helm charts or Kustomize overlays, describing the Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, and the exact image tag. There is typically a separate config repository per environment or an overlay per environment, so the Prod folder declares exactly what should run in Prod.

The controller runs inside the cluster and watches both Git and the live cluster. ArgoCD, for example, defines an `Application` resource pointing at a Git repo path and a target namespace. It periodically (and on webhook) fetches the manifests, computes a diff against the live objects, and if they differ it is "OutOfSync." Depending on policy it either shows the drift for a human to sync or, with automated sync enabled, applies the manifests itself to make the cluster match Git.

Drift correction is a core behaviour. If someone runs a manual `kubectl edit` to bump replicas in Prod, the controller detects that the live state no longer matches Git and, with self-heal enabled, reverts it back to what Git declares. This is impossible in a pure push model, where an out-of-band change simply persists unnoticed until it causes an incident.

Deployment in GitOps is a Git commit, not a kubectl command. The CI pipeline still builds and tests and produces an image tag, but instead of deploying, it opens a pull request (or commits) to the config repo updating the image tag for the target environment. Once that commit is merged, the controller notices and rolls it out. So the pipeline's job ends at "propose the desired state," and the controller owns "make it real."

Rollback becomes `git revert`. Because the cluster always reflects Git, reverting the commit that bumped the image tag causes the controller to roll the cluster back to the previous tag automatically. There is no separate rollback script and no risk of the rollback itself drifting, because Git remains the single truth.

Contrast with push-based Jenkins. There, Jenkins holds cluster credentials and runs `kubectl apply` or `helm upgrade` directly. The downsides are concrete: the record of what is actually deployed lives in Jenkins build logs rather than a reviewable Git history; any manual change to the cluster is invisible and permanent; rollback means re-running an old pipeline or a manual command; and Jenkins must store powerful cluster credentials, widening the attack surface.

A senior nuance is the security boundary. In GitOps the cluster credentials never leave the cluster, because the controller pulls from Git using read-only repo access, so an external CI breach cannot directly touch the cluster. Another nuance is that CI and CD are cleanly separated: CI produces artifacts and proposes state, the controller applies it. A third nuance is the "app of apps" or environment-promotion pattern, where promoting from QA to Prod is literally a commit copying a tested image tag from the QA overlay to the Prod overlay, which keeps promotion auditable and reversible.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India an engineer ran a manual kubectl command at 2 a.m. during an incident to bump the transfer service replicas, and forgot to put it back. Weeks later a deploy reset it and capacity silently dropped, causing a slowdown during peak hours. Nobody could tell what the cluster was supposed to look like. This is exactly the problem GitOps drift correction solves. The desired state lives in Git, and the controller would have flagged or reverted the manual change immediately so reality always matches the reviewed truth.

Problem 2 — A rollback of a bad fee change required an engineer to find and re-run an old Jenkins job, and under pressure they picked the wrong build number and made it worse. This is exactly the problem GitOps rollback solves. Reverting the Git commit that changed the image tag restores the exact previous declared state, and the controller rolls it back automatically.

Problem 3 — An auditor asked "what exactly is running in Prod right now and who approved it?" and the only answer was scattered Jenkins logs. This is exactly the problem GitOps auditability solves. The Prod folder in Git, plus its commit history and pull-request approvals, is a complete, reviewable record.

To make this concrete without a real cluster we will write a Java simulation. We will model a `GitRepo` holding the desired image tag (the source of truth), a `Cluster` holding the live image tag, and a `GitOpsController` that periodically reconciles the cluster toward Git, with self-heal that reverts drift. We will also model a `PushDeployer` representing the old Jenkins style for contrast. We will deploy via a Git commit and watch the controller apply it, simulate a manual drift and watch the controller heal it, then perform a `git revert` and watch the controller roll back. This mirrors the real pull-based reconciliation loop.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is an initial state where both Git and the cluster run `transfer-service:1.0.0`, followed by a deploy, a manual drift, a rollback, and a push-style deploy.

Step 1: CI proposes a new desired state by committing `transfer-service:1.1.0` to Git. At this moment Git says 1.1.0 but the cluster still runs 1.0.0, so they are out of sync.

Step 2: The controller reconciles. It compares desired (1.1.0) to live (1.0.0), finds them different, and because self-heal is on it applies 1.1.0 to the cluster. Now both match and the state is SYNCED.

Step 3: Someone runs a manual kubectl change, overriding the live cluster to `hotfix-manual`. Git still says 1.1.0, so the cluster has drifted away from the truth.

Step 4: The controller reconciles again. It sees the live tag no longer matches Git, flags OUT_OF_SYNC, and self-heals by reapplying 1.1.0, erasing the unauthorised manual change automatically.

Step 5: A rollback is needed, so an engineer does a git revert, popping the history back to 1.0.0. Git now declares 1.0.0 while the cluster runs 1.1.0.

Step 6: The controller reconciles and rolls the cluster back to 1.0.0 to match Git, with no rollback script needed. Finally, a push-style Jenkins deploy sets the live cluster to an untracked tag, but because Git still says 1.0.0, the very next reconcile heals it back, showing that in a GitOps world the controller, not an external push, has the final word.

```

2026-10-30 00:40:20 [WARNING] OUT_OF_SYNC: live=transfer-service:1.0.0 desired=transfer-service:1.1.0 -> healing
2026-10-30 00:40:20 [INFO] RECONCILED: cluster now runs transfer-service:1.1.0
2026-10-30 00:40:20 [INFO] === Drift: someone runs manual kubectl ===
2026-10-30 00:40:20 [WARNING] OUT_OF_SYNC: live=transfer-service:hotfix-manual desired=transfer-service:1.1.0 -> healing
2026-10-30 00:40:20 [INFO] RECONCILED: cluster now runs transfer-service:1.1.0
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
GitOps is an operational model where a Git repository holds the complete declared desired state of the system as manifests, and a controller running inside the cluster, such as ArgoCD or Flux, continuously compares the live cluster to that Git state and reconciles any difference. It is pull-based: the cluster converges itself toward Git rather than an outside tool pushing changes in. Deploying is no longer a kubectl command; it is a reviewed Git commit that updates the image tag, and the controller notices and rolls it out.

The differences from a push-based Jenkins deploy are concrete. Auditability is far stronger, because what is running is exactly what the Git history and its pull-request approvals say, rather than something buried in Jenkins build logs. Drift is corrected automatically, because if someone makes a manual change in the cluster the controller detects that the live state no longer matches Git and, with self-heal enabled, reverts it. Rollback is trivial, because reverting the commit that changed the image tag makes the controller roll the cluster back to the previous declared state, with no rollback script and no chance of the rollback itself drifting.

The security story is a major reason banks adopt it. In GitOps the cluster credentials never leave the cluster; the controller pulls from Git with read-only access, so a breach of the external CI system cannot directly touch the cluster. CI and CD are cleanly separated: CI builds and tests the artifact and proposes the new desired state, and the in-cluster controller owns actually applying it.

On the banking project we moved the transfer service from Jenkins running kubectl apply to ArgoCD watching a config repo. Deploys became commits that bumped the image tag in the Prod overlay, promotion from QA to Prod was a commit copying a tested tag between overlays, and rollback during an incident was a single git revert that ArgoCD applied automatically. The incident that originally motivated this was a 2 a.m. manual kubectl change that silently drifted and later caused a slowdown; with self-heal on, the controller would have reverted that drift within the next reconcile. The senior point I always add is that this eliminates the "what is actually running and who approved it" problem that auditors always ask about, because Git is the single, reviewable source of truth and the controller keeps reality honest.

answers.question: What deployment strategies do you use and how do they differ — rolling update, blue-green (two environments, instant switch + instant rollback), and canary (shift a % of traffic, observe, then ramp)?
answers.shortTitle: Deployment Strategies — Rolling Update, Blue-Green, and Canary

s1_definition.profdef: A deployment strategy is how you replace a running version of a service with a new one while controlling risk and downtime. A rolling update replaces instances gradually, a few at a time, so there is always capacity serving traffic and no downtime, but during the roll both versions run together. Blue-green keeps two complete environments, blue (current) and green (new); you deploy and test green fully, then flip a load balancer or router to send all traffic to green instantly, and roll back instantly by flipping back. Canary releases the new version to a small percentage of traffic first, observes metrics such as error rate and latency, and only ramps to 100% if the canary is healthy, otherwise it aborts.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of upgrading the teller counters at a National Bank of India branch. A rolling update is closing one counter at a time, upgrading it, and reopening it before touching the next, so the branch never fully closes but for a while some counters are old and some are new. Blue-green is building a second identical branch next door, fully fitting it out and testing it while the old one serves customers, then overnight redirecting everyone to the new branch with one sign change, and if anything is wrong you just point the sign back. Canary is sending only a handful of customers to the new counter first and watching closely; if they are served well you send more and more, but if they complain you quietly pull that counter before most customers ever saw it.
s1_definition.oneliner: Rolling swaps instances gradually with no downtime, blue-green flips all traffic between two full environments for instant switch and rollback, and canary shifts a small percentage first and ramps only if metrics stay healthy.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A deployment strategy is how you replace a running version of a service with a new one while controlling risk and downtime. A rolling update replaces instances gradually, a few at a time, so there is always capacity serving traffic and no downtime, but during the roll both versions run together. Blue-green keeps two complete environments, blue (current) and green (new); you deploy and test green fully, then flip a load balancer or router to send all traffic to green instantly, and roll back instantly by flipping back. Canary releases the new version to a small percentage of traffic first, observes metrics such as error rate and latency, and only ramps to 100% if the canary is healthy, otherwise it aborts.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of upgrading the teller counters at a National Bank of India branch. A rolling update is closing one counter at a time, upgrading it, and reopening it before touching the next, so the branch never fully closes but for a while some counters are old and some are new. Blue-green is building a second identical branch next door, fully fitting it out and testing it while the old one serves customers, then overnight redirecting everyone to the new branch with one sign change, and if anything is wrong you just point the sign back. Canary is sending only a handful of customers to the new counter first and watching closely; if they are served well you send more and more, but if they complain you quietly pull that counter before most customers ever saw it.

**One line to remember:** Rolling swaps instances gradually with no downtime, blue-green flips all traffic between two full environments for instant switch and rollback, and canary shifts a small percentage first and ramps only if metrics stay healthy.

sections.s2_technical:
A rolling update is the Kubernetes default. The Deployment has a `strategy` of type `RollingUpdate` with `maxUnavailable` and `maxSurge` controlling how many pods can be down and how many extra can be created during the roll. Kubernetes brings up new-version pods, waits for them to pass their readiness probe, then terminates old-version pods, repeating until all pods run the new version. The upside is no downtime and simple configuration. The nuance is that both versions serve traffic simultaneously during the roll, so the new version must be backward compatible with the old, especially for database schema and message formats, and rollback means rolling back the other way which takes time.

Blue-green uses two full environments. Blue runs the current version and takes all production traffic; green is a parallel environment where you deploy the new version and run full smoke and acceptance tests against it with no customer traffic. When green is verified, you switch the router or Service selector so all traffic goes to green at once. The switch is near-instant, and rollback is equally instant because you just point back to blue, which is still running untouched. The cost is you need double the capacity during the cutover, and like rolling, any shared database must be compatible with both versions during the overlap.

Canary is the most gradual and metric-driven. You deploy the new version alongside the old but route only a small slice of traffic to it, for example 5%, using a service mesh like Istio or an ingress weight. You then watch key signals: error rate, latency percentiles, and business metrics such as failed transfers. If the canary stays healthy you ramp the weight to 25%, 50%, then 100%; if any signal degrades you set the weight back to 0% and abort, so only a small fraction of users were ever affected. Canary gives the earliest, lowest-blast-radius detection of a bad release, at the cost of more tooling and automation to measure and decide.

Choosing between them depends on risk and infrastructure. Rolling is the sensible default for stateless services where brief version overlap is fine. Blue-green suits releases where you want a clean, instant, all-or-nothing switch and can afford double capacity, which is attractive for a core banking service during a tightly controlled release window. Canary suits high-traffic, high-risk changes where you want real production signal before full exposure, such as a change to the fraud-scoring model.

A senior nuance that applies to all three is database compatibility. Because old and new versions coexist (during the roll, during the blue-green overlap, or during the canary), schema changes must be done in backward-compatible steps, often called expand-and-contract: first add the new column or table without removing the old, deploy code that writes both, then only after full rollout remove the old. Another nuance is that readiness and health probes are what make these strategies safe; without an accurate readiness probe, Kubernetes will send traffic to a pod that is not actually ready. A third nuance is automated rollback: a mature canary ties the traffic weight to an automated analysis (for example with Argo Rollouts or Flagger) so a bad release is rolled back without a human in the loop.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India used to take the transfer service fully offline to deploy, causing a visible maintenance window during which Rajesh and Priya could not move money. Customers complained. This is exactly the problem a rolling update solves. Instances are replaced a few at a time while the rest keep serving, so there is no downtime.

Problem 2 — A risky rewrite of the settlement engine needed a clean, instant cutover with the ability to abort immediately if the ledger numbers looked wrong, because a partial rollout of a ledger change is dangerous. This is exactly the problem blue-green solves. The new engine runs fully in green, is verified against real data copies, and traffic flips all at once, with an instant flip back to blue if anything is off.

Problem 3 — A change to the fraud-scoring rules could either catch more fraud or wrongly block thousands of legitimate transfers, and the team could not know which until real traffic hit it. This is exactly the problem canary solves. Five percent of traffic goes to the new rules first while the team watches the false-decline rate, ramping up only if it stays healthy and aborting instantly if it spikes.

To make this concrete without a real cluster we will write a Java simulation of a traffic router. We will model a `Router` that splits requests between an old version and a new version by weight, a `RollingUpdate` that gradually shifts instances, a `BlueGreen` that flips all traffic at once, and a `Canary` that ramps weight while checking a health signal and aborts on degradation. We will run all three against a stream of transfer requests so you can see how each handles the transition and how canary aborts a bad release. This mirrors the real strategies without needing Istio.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is an old version at a 1% error rate and several new versions deployed with different strategies.

Step 1: The rolling update starts with a router sending 0% to new. In steps of 25% it shifts traffic: 25% new, then 50%, then 75%, then 100%. At each step both versions are live and serving, which is why the new version must be backward compatible. The roll finishes with 100% on the new version and no downtime at any point.

Step 2: The blue-green switch deploys green version 2.0.0 and runs smoke tests. Because green's error rate of 2% is below the 10% smoke-test threshold, it passes. The router then flips from 0% to 100% new in a single step, an instant all-or-nothing cutover, while blue remains running so a rollback would be instant.

Step 3: The healthy canary begins at 5% traffic to new version 1.1.0 and observes a 2% error rate, which is under the 5% abort threshold, so it ramps to 25%, then 50%, then 100%, staying healthy at every step and finishing promoted to 100%.

Step 4: The bad canary begins at 5% traffic to the broken fraud rules, observes a 30% error rate, which exceeds the 5% threshold, so it immediately sets the weight back to 0% and aborts. Only the 5% slice ever saw the bad version, and no further ramp happened.

A deployment strategy is how I replace a running version with a new one while controlling risk and downtime, and I pick from three main approaches. A rolling update replaces instances gradually, a few at a time, so there is always capacity serving traffic and no downtime; its trade-off is that both versions run together during the roll, so the new version must be backward compatible. Canary suits high-risk, high-traffic changes such as a new fraud-scoring model, where I need real production signal before exposing everyone.

The one point I always stress because it applies to all three is database compatibility. Since old and new versions coexist during the roll, the blue-green overlap, or the canary, schema changes must be done in backward-compatible, expand-and-contract steps: add the new column first, deploy code that writes both old and new, and only remove the old column after the rollout is complete. I also rely on accurate readiness probes, because they are what stop Kubernetes from sending traffic to a pod that is not truly ready.

On the banking project I used rolling for most stateless services, blue-green for a risky settlement-engine rewrite so we could flip and, if the ledger numbers looked wrong, flip straight back, and canary with Argo Rollouts for a fraud-rules change where a bad release could wrongly block thousands of legitimate transfers. The senior point I always add is that the canary was wired to automated metric analysis, so if the false-decline rate spiked it rolled back to zero percent on its own without waiting for a human, which is exactly the safety you want when real customers' money is involved.

answers.question: The CI stage succeeds but the CD stage fails — how do you debug it, where do you check pipeline logs, and how do you roll back a failed deployment safely?
answers.shortTitle: Scenario — CI Succeeds but CD Fails: Debugging, Where to Check Logs, and Safe Rollback

s1_definition.profdef: When CI passes but CD fails, the problem is almost never the code's correctness (CI proved that) but rather the deployment itself: a bad manifest, a missing secret or config, an image that cannot be pulled, a failing readiness probe, insufficient cluster resources, or an environment-specific dependency being unreachable. Debugging means reading the CD pipeline logs first, then the platform's view of the rollout (`kubectl rollout status`, pod events, and container logs), identifying whether the new version ever became healthy, and then rolling back safely to the last known-good version using the platform's rollback mechanism while keeping the failed version's evidence for analysis.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India certified a batch of cheques as valid (CI passed) but the courier failed to deliver them to the destination branch (CD failed). The cheques are fine; the delivery broke. To debug, you first read the courier's trip log (the CD pipeline log), then ask the destination branch what they saw at the door (the cluster events and pod logs): was the address wrong (bad manifest), was the gate locked (missing secret), did the parcel never arrive (image pull failed), or did the branch reject it on inspection (readiness probe failing)? To make customers safe again, you immediately revert to the previous known-good delivery while you investigate, rather than leaving customers stranded.
s1_definition.oneliner: CI passing but CD failing means the code is fine but the deployment broke, so read the CD log then the cluster's rollout status, pod events and container logs, and roll back to the last known-good version immediately while preserving the evidence.

Debugging means reading the CD pipeline logs first, then the platform's view of the rollout (`kubectl rollout status`, pod events, and container logs), identifying whether the new version ever became healthy, and then rolling back safely to the last known-good version using the platform's rollback mechanism while keeping the failed version's evidence for analysis.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India certified a batch of cheques as valid (CI passed) but the courier failed to deliver them to the destination branch (CD failed). The cheques are fine; the delivery broke. To debug, you first read the courier's trip log (the CD pipeline log), then ask the destination branch what they saw at the door (the cluster events and pod logs): was the address wrong (bad manifest), was the gate locked (missing secret), did the parcel never arrive (image pull failed), or did the branch reject it on inspection (readiness probe failing)?
