sections.s6_takeaway:
Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes, and it solves the problem of managing raw manifests by hand across many environments. A Helm chart is a versioned bundle of templated manifests plus a default values file. The templates use Go templating to substitute values, so a single chart can render a two-replica Deployment pointing at a dev database or a ten-replica Deployment pointing at a production database, purely by supplying a different values file. That eliminates the configuration drift that happens when you maintain separate copies of YAML per environment.

Parameterization works through layered values. I keep base defaults in the chart's values file and layer environment-specific overrides such as a production values file that bumps replicas, resource requests, and the database host. At deploy time I select the overlay with a flag, so dev, staging, and production all come from the same template with no divergence in structure, only in the injected values.

Versioning is deliberately two-dimensional. The chart version tracks the package itself and changes when templates or defaults change, while the app version tracks the application image the chart deploys. Keeping them separate means I can ship a chart fix, like adding a readiness probe, without pretending the application changed, and I can roll out a new application image without altering chart structure. Charts are published to a repository and consumed by version, which makes every deployment reproducible and auditable.

The lifecycle commands map to tracked revisions, and that is what makes Helm powerful operationally. Install creates a named release at revision one, upgrade applies changes and records a new revision, the history command lists every revision with its chart version and status, and rollback reverts to a chosen revision in a single command. In my banking project at the National Bank of India I always deploy production with the atomic flag, so a failed upgrade automatically rolls back to the last good release instead of leaving production half-broken. That turned a tense, manual YAML hunt during an incident into a one-command recovery, while a single parameterized chart ensured dev, staging, and production never drifted apart again.

answers.question: (Scenario) A pod is stuck in `CrashLoopBackOff` / `ImagePullBackOff` / `Pending` / `ContainerCreating` — how do you diagnose each (`kubectl describe`, `logs --previous`, events, image/registry creds, resource requests vs node capacity, PVC binding)?
answers.shortTitle: (Scenario) Diagnosing CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff, Pending, and ContainerCreating

s1_definition.profdef: These are four distinct Pod phases that signal four different failure classes. CrashLoopBackOff means the container starts and then exits repeatedly, so the application itself is failing after launch. ImagePullBackOff means the kubelet cannot pull the container image, usually a wrong tag or missing registry credentials. Pending means the scheduler cannot place the Pod on any node, usually insufficient CPU or memory, taints, or an unbound volume claim. ContainerCreating means the Pod is scheduled but the kubelet is still setting it up, typically waiting on image pull, volume mount, or a Secret. You diagnose them with `kubectl describe pod` for events, `kubectl logs --previous` for the last crash, and checks of registry credentials, node capacity, and volume binding.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, CrashLoopBackOff is a teller who sits down and immediately faints, over and over. ImagePullBackOff is a teller who cannot even get their uniform because the supply room door is locked or the uniform does not exist. Pending is a teller with no desk because the branch is full. ContainerCreating is a teller who has a desk and is still unpacking their drawer before opening the counter. Each needs a completely different fix, so the first job is to read the events to learn which story you are in.
s1_definition.oneliner: CrashLoopBackOff is the app crashing after start, ImagePullBackOff is the image not pulling, Pending is the scheduler finding no room, and ContainerCreating is setup in progress, each diagnosed from describe events and logs.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** These are four distinct Pod phases that signal four different failure classes. CrashLoopBackOff means the container starts and then exits repeatedly, so the application itself is failing after launch. ImagePullBackOff means the kubelet cannot pull the container image, usually a wrong tag or missing registry credentials. Pending means the scheduler cannot place the Pod on any node, usually insufficient CPU or memory, taints, or an unbound volume claim. ContainerCreating means the Pod is scheduled but the kubelet is still setting it up, typically waiting on image pull, volume mount, or a Secret. You diagnose them with `kubectl describe pod` for events, `kubectl logs --previous` for the last crash, and checks of registry credentials, node capacity, and volume binding.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, CrashLoopBackOff is a teller who sits down and immediately faints, over and over. ImagePullBackOff is a teller who cannot even get their uniform because the supply room door is locked or the uniform does not exist. Pending is a teller with no desk because the branch is full. ContainerCreating is a teller who has a desk and is still unpacking their drawer before opening the counter. Each needs a completely different fix, so the first job is to read the events to learn which story you are in.

**One line to remember:** CrashLoopBackOff is the app crashing after start, ImagePullBackOff is the image not pulling, Pending is the scheduler finding no room, and ContainerCreating is setup in progress, each diagnosed from describe events and logs.

sections.s2_technical:
For CrashLoopBackOff, the container launches, the process exits, the kubelet restarts it with exponential backoff, and the state cycles. The key tool is `kubectl logs <pod> --previous`, because the current container may be too young to have logs; the `--previous` flag shows the output of the crashed instance, where you usually find the stack trace, a missing environment variable, a failed database connection, or a bad command. I also run `kubectl describe pod` to read the last state and exit code. Common banking causes are a wrong JDBC URL, a missing Secret, a failed Flyway migration at boot, or an out-of-memory kill right after startup.

For ImagePullBackOff, the scheduler placed the Pod but the kubelet cannot fetch the image. `kubectl describe pod` shows an event like "Failed to pull image" with the reason. The usual causes are a typo in the image name or tag, the tag not existing in the registry, or missing registry credentials, which in a private bank registry means the `imagePullSecrets` is absent or wrong. The fix is to correct the tag, confirm the image exists, and attach a valid pull secret to the Pod's service account.

For Pending, the Pod is not scheduled at all. `kubectl describe pod` shows FailedScheduling events explaining why: insufficient CPU or memory on all nodes, a node selector or affinity rule matching nothing, a taint the Pod does not tolerate, or a PersistentVolumeClaim that cannot bind. I compare the Pod's resource requests to node allocatable capacity with `kubectl describe node`, and I check `kubectl get pvc` for an unbound claim. The fix is to lower requests, add capacity (often via the Cluster Autoscaler), fix the selector or toleration, or provision a matching volume.

For ContainerCreating, the Pod is scheduled and the kubelet is working through setup. `kubectl describe pod` events reveal what it is waiting on: still pulling the image, mounting a volume, attaching a cloud disk, or fetching a referenced Secret or ConfigMap that does not exist. A Pod stuck here for a long time usually means a missing Secret, a volume that will not attach, or a CNI problem assigning a Pod IP. The senior discipline across all four is identical: always start with `kubectl describe pod` to read the Events section, because the events almost always name the exact cause, and only then reach for logs or node and volume inspection.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India our Transfer Service deployment hit all four of these states on different days. The scenario reproduces each with its real cause and fix.

Problem 1 — a release pointed at image tag v9 which was never pushed, so Pods sat in ImagePullBackOff. The fix was correcting the tag and attaching the registry pull secret.

Problem 2 — a bad boot where the database password Secret was missing caused the app to throw on startup and land in CrashLoopBackOff. The previous-container logs showed the exact exception.

Problem 3 — the Pod requested 4 CPUs but every node had at most 2 free, so it stayed Pending until we lowered the request and let the Cluster Autoscaler add a node.

Problem 4 — a Pod referenced a volume whose PersistentVolumeClaim was not yet bound, so it stuck in ContainerCreating until the claim bound.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `PodDiagnostician` that models a Pod moving through these phases and, for each stuck phase, emits the same evidence a real `kubectl describe` plus `logs --previous` would show, then prints the fix. It uses the `Account` model for Rajesh and Priya so that once the Pod is healthy a transfer runs, proving the fix worked.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four Pod specs each engineered to hit one stuck phase, plus one healthy spec.

Step 1 — The Pending case requests 4 CPUs on nodes with 2 free. The diagnostician emits a FailedScheduling event showing insufficient CPU and returns Pending. The fix is to lower the request or let the Cluster Autoscaler add a node.

Step 2 — The ContainerCreating case has an unbound PersistentVolumeClaim. The diagnostician emits an "unable to attach volume" event and returns ContainerCreating. The fix is to provision a matching volume or fix the StorageClass.

Step 3 — The ImagePullBackOff case points at image tag v9, which does not exist. The diagnostician emits a "Failed to pull image" event naming the missing tag and returns ImagePullBackOff. The fix is to correct the tag, push the image, or attach the pull secret.

Step 4 — The CrashLoopBackOff case is missing the database password Secret. The container starts and immediately exits with code 1. The diagnostician shows the last terminated state and the previous-container log line with the IllegalStateException, and returns CrashLoopBackOff. The fix is to create the Secret and restart.

Step 5 — The healthy spec passes every check and returns Running, so a transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya executes successfully, confirming that once the right fix is applied the Pod serves traffic.

CrashLoopBackOff means the container launches and then the process exits repeatedly, so the application itself is failing after start. The crucial tool here is viewing the previous container's logs, because the current attempt may be too young to have output, and the previous logs usually hold the stack trace, a missing environment variable, a failed database connection, or a boot-time migration error. ImagePullBackOff means the kubelet cannot fetch the image at all, and describe shows a failed-to-pull event whose cause is almost always a wrong tag, a tag that was never pushed, or a missing registry pull secret, so I correct the tag, confirm the image exists, and attach a valid pull secret.

Pending means the scheduler could not place the Pod on any node, and the failed-scheduling event explains why, whether that is insufficient CPU or memory, a node selector or affinity that matches nothing, a taint the Pod does not tolerate, or a volume claim that cannot bind. I compare the Pod's resource requests against node allocatable capacity and I check the claim, then I either lower the requests, let the Cluster Autoscaler add a node, fix the selector or toleration, or provision the volume. ContainerCreating means the Pod was scheduled and the kubelet is still setting it up, so the events tell me what it is waiting on, typically a slow image pull, a volume that will not attach, or a referenced Secret or ConfigMap that does not exist.

In my project at the National Bank of India our Transfer Service hit all four in different weeks. A release pointed at an image tag we never pushed and every Pod went into ImagePullBackOff. A missing database-password Secret made the app throw on boot and land in CrashLoopBackOff, which the previous-container logs pinpointed instantly. An oversized CPU request left a Pod Pending until we trimmed it and the autoscaler added a node. And an unbound volume claim froze a Pod in ContainerCreating until the claim bound. The common thread is discipline: read the events first, then reach for previous logs, node capacity, registry credentials, or volume binding depending on exactly which state the Pod is stuck in, and never restart Pods blindly hoping the problem goes away.

answers.question: (Scenario) Pods are `Running` but not receiving traffic via the Ingress/Service — walk through the layers (readiness probe, Service selector/endpoints, Ingress rules, NetworkPolicy, LB health checks).
answers.shortTitle: (Scenario) Pods Are Running but Receive No Traffic Through Ingress/Service

s1_definition.profdef: When Pods are Running but get no traffic, the containers are healthy yet something between the client and the Pod is broken. The diagnosis walks the request path layer by layer: the readiness probe must pass so the Pod is marked Ready, the Service selector must match the Pod labels so the EndpointSlice lists the Pod IP, the Ingress host and path rules must point at the right Service and port, any NetworkPolicy must allow the traffic, and the external load balancer health checks must consider the backend healthy.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India the teller is at the desk and ready to serve, but no customers arrive. The teller being present is "Running." The missing customers could be because the OPEN sign never flipped on (readiness), the branch directory lists the wrong desk number (Service selector and endpoints), the reception sends "transfers" visitors to the wrong floor (Ingress rules), a security door blocks the corridor (NetworkPolicy), or the building's front-gate guard marked this branch "closed" on his sheet (load balancer health check). You check each checkpoint from the street inward until you find the broken one.
s1_definition.oneliner: Running means the container is alive, not reachable; trace readiness, Service selector and endpoints, Ingress rules, NetworkPolicy, and load balancer health checks until you find the gap.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When Pods are Running but get no traffic, the containers are healthy yet something between the client and the Pod is broken. The diagnosis walks the request path layer by layer: the readiness probe must pass so the Pod is marked Ready, the Service selector must match the Pod labels so the EndpointSlice lists the Pod IP, the Ingress host and path rules must point at the right Service and port, any NetworkPolicy must allow the traffic, and the external load balancer health checks must consider the backend healthy.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India the teller is at the desk and ready to serve, but no customers arrive. The teller being present is "Running." The missing customers could be because the OPEN sign never flipped on (readiness), the branch directory lists the wrong desk number (Service selector and endpoints), the reception sends "transfers" visitors to the wrong floor (Ingress rules), a security door blocks the corridor (NetworkPolicy), or the building's front-gate guard marked this branch "closed" on his sheet (load balancer health check). You check each checkpoint from the street inward until you find the broken one.

**One line to remember:** Running means the container is alive, not reachable; trace readiness, Service selector and endpoints, Ingress rules, NetworkPolicy, and load balancer health checks until you find the gap.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with readiness, because a Running Pod whose readiness probe fails is deliberately kept out of the Service. I run `kubectl get pods` and look at the READY column; if it shows 0/1 even though STATUS is Running, the readiness probe is failing and the Pod is correctly excluded from traffic. The fix is to make the readiness endpoint pass.

Next check the Service selector and endpoints. The Service selects Pods by labels, and the EndpointSlice controller lists the IPs of matching ready Pods. If the Service selector is `app=transfer` but the Pods are labelled `app=transfer-service`, the selector matches nothing and the endpoint list is empty, so traffic has nowhere to go. I run `kubectl get endpointslices` or `kubectl describe service` and confirm the endpoint list is non-empty and contains the Pod IPs. An empty list is the single most common cause and usually traces back to a label mismatch or failing readiness.

Then verify the Service plumbing itself: the Service `port` versus `targetPort` must match the container's actual listening port. A Service forwarding port 80 to targetPort 8080 only works if the container listens on 8080. I test inside the cluster with a temporary Pod doing `curl http://transfer-service:80` to isolate whether the Service works before blaming the Ingress.

Next the Ingress. The Ingress host and path rules must name the correct Service and port, and the Ingress controller must actually be running and have an address. I run `kubectl describe ingress` to confirm the backend is the right Service and `kubectl get ingress` to confirm it has an external address. A wrong service name, a path that does not match, or a missing IngressClass are typical breaks.

Then NetworkPolicy. In a locked-down banking namespace a default-deny policy can block ingress to the Pods unless an explicit allow rule permits traffic from the Ingress controller's namespace or Pod labels. I check `kubectl get networkpolicy` and confirm there is an allow rule for the relevant source.

Finally the external load balancer health checks. For a LoadBalancer Service or a cloud Ingress, the cloud load balancer runs its own health checks against the node ports or target group. If those health checks hit a path that returns non-200, the load balancer marks the backend unhealthy and sends no traffic even though Kubernetes thinks everything is fine. I check the cloud target group health in the provider console. The senior discipline is to test from the inside out: curl the Pod IP directly, then the Service, then through the Ingress, then from outside, so each hop tells you whether the break is below or above it.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India our Transfer Service Pods were Running after a deploy, but the mobile app got timeouts. The scenario reproduces the layered walk that found the break.

Problem 1 — a refactor renamed the Pod label from `app=transfer` to `app=transfer-svc`, but the Service selector still said `app=transfer`, so the endpoint list was empty and no traffic flowed even though Pods were Running and Ready. This is the classic selector mismatch.

Problem 2 — separately, a readiness probe pointed at the wrong path returned 404, so Pods showed 0/1 Ready and were excluded. Both faults produce the same symptom, which is why a layered walk is essential.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `TrafficPathChecker` that models each layer: readiness, Service selector versus Pod labels and the resulting endpoints, Ingress backend mapping, NetworkPolicy allow rules, and load balancer health. It walks the layers in order, reports the first broken one with the fix, and once every layer is healthy routes a transfer for Rajesh and Priya to prove traffic reaches the Pod.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a Running, Ready Pod labelled `app=transfer-svc`, first fronted by a Service whose selector wrongly says `app=transfer`, then by a corrected Service.

Step 1 — Layer 1 readiness: the Pod is Ready, so it is not excluded for readiness reasons. The walk continues.

Step 2 — Layer 2 endpoints: the Service selector `app=transfer` is compared to the Pod labels `app=transfer-svc`. They do not match, so the endpoint list is empty. The checker reports the empty-endpoints break and the fix to align the selector, and stops. This reproduces the real outage: Pods Running and Ready, yet zero traffic.

Step 3 — We apply the fix by using a Service whose selector is `app=transfer-svc`. The walk runs again. Readiness passes, the selector now matches so the endpoint list contains the Pod IP, and the targetPort 8080 matches the container's listen port.

Step 4 — Layer 3 Ingress: the Ingress backend names `transfer-service`, which matches the actual Service, so routing is correct. Layer 4 NetworkPolicy allows ingress from the controller. Layer 5 load balancer health check passes.

Step 5 — Every layer is healthy, so traffic reaches the Pod IP. A transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya is routed to the Pod and succeeds, proving the end-to-end path is restored.

sections.s6_takeaway:
When Pods are Running but receive no traffic, the containers themselves are healthy and the fault lies somewhere between the client and the Pod, so I walk the request path layer by layer rather than guessing. My golden rule is to test from the inside out: curl the Pod directly, then the Service, then through the Ingress, then from outside, because each successful hop tells me the break is above it and each failed hop tells me the break is at or below it.

I start with readiness, because a Running Pod whose readiness probe is failing is deliberately excluded from the Service and shows zero-slash-one in the ready column. Next I check the Service selector against the Pod labels and look at the endpoint list, because an empty endpoint list is by far the most common cause and almost always traces back to a label mismatch or failing readiness. While there, I confirm the Service target port matches the container's real listening port. Then I inspect the Ingress to make sure its host and path rules point at the correct Service and port and that the Ingress controller actually has an address. After that I check for a default-deny NetworkPolicy that blocks ingress from the controller, which is common in locked-down banking namespaces. Finally I check the external load balancer's own health checks, because a cloud load balancer that gets a non-200 from its health path will mark the backend unhealthy and send no traffic even though Kubernetes believes everything is fine.

The reason this layered approach matters is that several completely different faults produce the exact same symptom of Running Pods with no traffic, so a methodical walk is faster and safer than trial and error. In my project at the National Bank of India a refactor renamed the Pod label but left the Service selector pointing at the old label, so the endpoint list went empty and the mobile app timed out even though every Pod was Running and Ready. Aligning the Service selector with the new Pod labels restored the endpoints instantly and traffic flowed again. That incident is exactly why I always inspect endpoints early and verify each layer in order instead of restarting Pods that were never actually broken.

answers.question: What causes `OOMKilled` even when monitoring looks normal (container memory limit vs JVM heap/off-heap, container-aware JVM flags), and how do you right-size requests/limits?
answers.shortTitle: Why Pods Get OOMKilled Even When Monitoring Looks Normal, and Right-Sizing Requests/Limits

s1_definition.profdef: OOMKilled means the Linux kernel's out-of-memory killer terminated a container because its cgroup memory usage exceeded the container's memory limit. It can happen even when heap dashboards look fine because the container limit caps total process memory, which includes the JVM heap plus off-heap memory such as thread stacks, metaspace, code cache, direct byte buffers, and native allocations. Right-sizing means setting the memory request to the typical working set and the limit above the real peak, and making the JVM container-aware so its heap sizing respects the cgroup limit rather than the whole node.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, imagine a teller's cubicle has a strict space limit for everything they bring in. Your dashboard only measures the papers on the desk (the JVM heap), but the cubicle limit counts the desk papers plus the filing cabinet, the chair, the coat rack, and the coffee machine (off-heap and native memory). So the cubicle can overflow and security evicts the teller even though the desk papers looked modest on the report. The fix is to measure the whole cubicle, not just the desk, and to tell the teller how big the cubicle actually is so they do not bring a desk sized for a whole floor.
s1_definition.oneliner: OOMKilled is the cgroup limit cap on TOTAL memory (heap plus off-heap plus native), not just the heap your dashboard shows, so size limits to real peak and make the JVM container-aware.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** OOMKilled means the Linux kernel's out-of-memory killer terminated a container because its cgroup memory usage exceeded the container's memory limit. It can happen even when heap dashboards look fine because the container limit caps total process memory, which includes the JVM heap plus off-heap memory such as thread stacks, metaspace, code cache, direct byte buffers, and native allocations. Right-sizing means setting the memory request to the typical working set and the limit above the real peak, and making the JVM container-aware so its heap sizing respects the cgroup limit rather than the whole node.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, imagine a teller's cubicle has a strict space limit for everything they bring in. Your dashboard only measures the papers on the desk (the JVM heap), but the cubicle limit counts the desk papers plus the filing cabinet, the chair, the coat rack, and the coffee machine (off-heap and native memory). So the cubicle can overflow and security evicts the teller even though the desk papers looked modest on the report. The fix is to measure the whole cubicle, not just the desk, and to tell the teller how big the cubicle actually is so they do not bring a desk sized for a whole floor.

**One line to remember:** OOMKilled is the cgroup limit cap on TOTAL memory (heap plus off-heap plus native), not just the heap your dashboard shows, so size limits to real peak and make the JVM container-aware.

sections.s2_technical:
A container's memory limit is enforced by the Linux cgroup. When the sum of all memory the process touches crosses that limit, the kernel kills the process with signal 9 and Kubernetes records the container's last state as OOMKilled with exit code 137. The critical insight is what counts toward that limit: it is the entire resident memory of the JVM process, not just the Java heap. The heap is only one region. Off-heap and native memory also count, including thread stacks (each thread costs around half a megabyte to a megabyte), metaspace for class metadata, the JIT code cache, direct byte buffers used heavily by Netty and NIO, memory-mapped files, and native allocations by libraries.

This is exactly why monitoring can look normal. If your dashboard graphs only heap usage and the heap sits comfortably at sixty percent, you conclude everything is fine, but the container still gets OOMKilled because thread stacks, metaspace, and direct buffers pushed total resident memory past the limit. A thread leak that spawns thousands of threads, or a direct-buffer leak, will OOM-kill a container while the heap graph stays flat.

The JVM flags matter enormously. Older JVMs read the host machine's total memory, not the container limit, so inside a container with a one-gigabyte limit an old JVM might size its default heap for a thirty-two-gigabyte node and get killed immediately. Modern JVMs are container-aware by default, honoring the cgroup limit. I still set it explicitly with `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage`, which tells the JVM to size the maximum heap as a percentage of the container limit, for example seventy-five percent, leaving the remaining quarter for off-heap and native memory. I avoid hardcoding `-Xmx` to a fixed value that ignores the limit, and I never set the heap equal to the whole container limit because that leaves nothing for the rest.

Right-sizing requests and limits is a measurement exercise. The request is what the scheduler reserves and should reflect the typical working set so Pods schedule sensibly; the limit is the hard cap and should sit above the observed real peak of total memory with some headroom. I measure actual usage under realistic load using container memory metrics, not just heap, then set the request near the steady state and the limit comfortably above the peak. I also understand QoS implications: when request equals limit the Pod is Guaranteed and is the last to be evicted under node pressure, whereas a Burstable Pod with request below limit is more exposed. For a banking service I lean toward Guaranteed memory for the critical path. The senior discipline is to profile native memory with Native Memory Tracking when heap looks innocent, because a flat heap graph combined with OOMKills almost always means an off-heap or native leak.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India our Transfer Service kept getting OOMKilled in production while the heap dashboard showed a healthy sixty percent. The scenario reproduces the hidden-memory trap.

Problem 1 — the container limit was one gigabyte and we set the heap to nearly a gigabyte, leaving almost nothing for thread stacks, metaspace, and the direct buffers our HTTP client used. Under load, total memory crossed the limit and the container was OOMKilled with exit code 137, even though heap was fine. This is exactly the heap-versus-total confusion.

Problem 2 — an older base image used a JVM that sized the heap from the node's thirty-two gigabytes, ignoring the one-gigabyte limit, so the Pod died on startup. The fix was a container-aware JVM with MaxRAMPercentage.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `ContainerMemoryModel` that tracks heap plus off-heap plus native against a cgroup limit, an `OomKiller` that fires when total crosses the limit, and a `JvmSizer` that computes a safe max heap from the limit using a RAM percentage. We run a transfer for Rajesh and Priya under a badly-sized config (OOMKilled) and a right-sized config (succeeds), logging the breakdown.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a one-gigabyte container limit, first with an oversized heap and then with a container-aware heap.

Step 1 — Under the bad config, the heap is set to 960 MiB. The dashboard would show only this heap and it looks reasonable against the limit. But the model adds metaspace of 96, thread stacks of 80, and direct buffers of 120, giving a total of 1256 MiB.

Step 2 — The OOM killer compares the total of 1256 MiB to the limit of 1024 MiB. The total exceeds the limit, so the kernel sends SIGKILL and the container is OOMKilled with exit code 137. The log stresses that the heap looked fine, which is the exact real-world confusion.

Step 3 — We switch to a container-aware configuration. The JvmSizer computes the max heap as seventy-five percent of the one-gigabyte limit, which is 768 MiB, deliberately leaving a quarter of the limit for off-heap and native memory.

Step 4 — The good model uses a heap of 768 MiB plus metaspace 96, thread stacks 80, and direct buffers 60, for a total of 1004 MiB, which is just under the 1024 MiB limit.

Step 5 — The OOM killer sees the total within the limit, so the container stays up. A transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya runs successfully, proving that leaving headroom for off-heap memory prevents the kill while still using most of the limit for heap.

Final output:

```

2026-10-30 00:59:40.101 [SEVERE] OOMKilled: total 1256MiB > limit 1024MiB — SIGKILL, exit code 137 (heap looked fine!)
2026-10-30 00:59:40.102 [INFO] transfer attempt under BAD sizing killed=true
2026-10-30 00:59:40.103 [INFO] JVM container-aware: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 on limit 1024MiB -> maxHeap=768MiB
2026-10-30 00:59:40.104 [INFO] mem: heap=768 meta=96 stacks=80 direct=60 TOTAL=1004MiB / limit=1024MiB (dashboard shows only heap=768)
2026-10-30 00:59:40.105 [INFO] memory within limit — container stays up
2026-10-30 00:59:40.106 [INFO] transfer SAV2001->CUR3001 Rs.50000 SUCCESS under right-sized memory
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
OOMKilled means the Linux kernel's out-of-memory killer terminated a container because its cgroup memory usage crossed the container's memory limit, and Kubernetes records that as exit code 137. The reason it can happen while monitoring looks perfectly normal is that most dashboards graph only the Java heap, but the container limit caps the entire resident memory of the process. That total includes the heap plus a lot of off-heap and native memory: thread stacks, metaspace for class metadata, the JIT code cache, direct byte buffers used heavily by networking libraries, memory-mapped files, and native allocations. So the heap can sit at a comfortable sixty percent while thread stacks and direct buffers quietly push the total past the limit and get the container killed.

The JVM flags are central to avoiding this. Older JVMs read the host machine's memory rather than the container limit, so inside a one-gigabyte container an old JVM might size its heap for a thirty-two-gigabyte node and die immediately. Modern JVMs are container-aware, and I make it explicit by setting the maximum heap as a percentage of the container limit, typically seventy-five percent, which deliberately leaves the remaining quarter for off-heap and native memory. I never set the heap equal to the whole limit, because that starves everything else and guarantees an OOM kill under load.

Right-sizing requests and limits is a measurement exercise rather than a guess. The request is what the scheduler reserves and should match the typical working set so Pods schedule sensibly, while the limit is the hard cap and should sit above the real observed peak of total memory with some headroom. I measure actual container memory under realistic load, not just heap, and for a critical banking path I often set request equal to limit so the Pod gets Guaranteed quality of service and is the last to be evicted under node pressure.

In my project at the National Bank of India our Transfer Service kept getting OOMKilled while the heap dashboard showed a healthy sixty percent. The cause was that we had sized the heap at nearly the full one-gigabyte limit, leaving no room for thread stacks, metaspace, and the direct buffers our HTTP client allocated, so total memory crossed the limit even though heap looked fine. Setting the heap to seventy-five percent of the limit with a container-aware flag, graphing the container's total working set instead of just the heap, and using Native Memory Tracking to confirm there was no native leak, eliminated the kills while still using most of the limit productively.

answers.question: What are Kubernetes QoS classes (Guaranteed = requests==limits, Burstable = requests<limits, BestEffort = none), how do they affect which pods are OOM-killed first under node memory pressure, and why is `emptyDir` volume data lost when a pod is restarted/rescheduled (it's tied to the pod lifecycle)?
answers.shortTitle: Kubernetes QoS Classes, OOM Eviction Order, and Why emptyDir Data Is Lost

s1_definition.profdef: Kubernetes assigns each Pod a Quality of Service class based on its resource requests and limits. Guaranteed means every container sets requests equal to limits for both CPU and memory. Burstable means at least one container sets a request but not equal-limits for all resources. BestEffort means no requests or limits at all. Under node memory pressure the kubelet evicts in the order BestEffort first, then Burstable that exceed their requests, and Guaranteed last, and the OOM killer uses a correlated oom_score so BestEffort processes are killed before Guaranteed ones. An emptyDir volume shares the Pod's lifecycle, so its data is created when the Pod is assigned to a node and deleted when the Pod is removed or rescheduled, which is why its contents do not survive a reschedule.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, when the branch runs short of space, management decides who gets moved out first. BestEffort tellers made no reservation, so they are moved first. Burstable tellers reserved a small desk but spread onto extra space, so they are moved next if they overflowed their reservation. Guaranteed tellers reserved exactly the space they use, so they are protected and moved last. An emptyDir is a scratch notepad clipped to the teller's badge; the moment that teller leaves the building the notepad is thrown away, so nothing written on it survives their departure.
s1_definition.oneliner: Guaranteed Pods survive longest and BestEffort die first under memory pressure, and emptyDir is scratch space tied to the Pod, so it vanishes on restart or reschedule.

sections.s2_technical:
The QoS class is derived, not set directly. If every container in the Pod specifies both a memory request and limit and both a CPU request and limit, and the requests equal the limits, the Pod is Guaranteed. If the Pod has at least one request or limit set but does not meet the strict equality for all containers and resources, it is Burstable. If no container sets any request or limit, it is BestEffort. You can see the class with `kubectl get pod -o jsonpath` on the status QoS field or in `kubectl describe pod`.

The class drives eviction under node memory pressure. When a node runs low on allocatable memory, the kubelet begins evicting Pods to reclaim it, and it ranks candidates so BestEffort Pods go first because they reserved nothing, then Burstable Pods that are using more than their requests, and Guaranteed Pods last. Separately, the Linux OOM killer assigns each process an oom_score_adj that Kubernetes sets according to QoS, so if the kernel itself has to kill a process, a BestEffort container has a much higher kill priority than a Guaranteed one. The practical lesson for banking is to make critical services Guaranteed by setting requests equal to limits, so a noisy BestEffort batch job cannot cause the kubelet to evict the Transfer Service first.

A subtlety is that CPU and memory behave differently. CPU is compressible, so exceeding a CPU limit throttles the container rather than killing it. Memory is incompressible, so exceeding a memory limit gets the container OOMKilled, and under node pressure the QoS ranking decides who is evicted. That is why memory requests and limits deserve the most care.

The emptyDir question is about lifecycle. An emptyDir volume is created empty when the Pod is scheduled to a node and lives on that node's disk, or in memory if the medium is memory. Its lifetime is exactly the Pod's lifetime on that node. If a container in the Pod restarts, the emptyDir survives because the Pod is still the same Pod on the same node. But if the Pod itself is deleted, evicted, or rescheduled to a different node, the emptyDir and everything in it are gone, because the Pod it belonged to no longer exists and a brand-new Pod gets a brand-new empty emptyDir. This is why emptyDir is correct for scratch data like a cache, a temporary download, or a scratch space shared between containers in the same Pod, but completely wrong for anything that must persist. For durable data in a bank, such as a ledger or uploaded documents, I use a PersistentVolumeClaim backed by a PersistentVolume, whose lifecycle is independent of any Pod, so the data survives Pod restarts, reschedules, and even node loss. The senior discipline is to match the volume type to the durability requirement: emptyDir for ephemeral scratch, PersistentVolumeClaim for durable state, and a StatefulSet with per-replica claims for stateful workloads.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India two incidents taught us about QoS and emptyDir.

Problem 1 — a BestEffort nightly report job with no limits ballooned in memory and caused node pressure, and the kubelet evicted our Transfer Service first because the Transfer Service was Burstable at the time. We made the Transfer Service Guaranteed so it would be protected. This is exactly the eviction-order lesson.

Problem 2 — a developer cached generated account statements in an emptyDir to speed up re-downloads. When the Pod rescheduled to another node during a deploy, every cached statement vanished and users re-generated them, which was fine for a cache but would have been catastrophic if that data had been the only copy. This is exactly the emptyDir lifecycle lesson, and it is why the authoritative statements live in a PersistentVolume.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `QosClassifier` that derives the QoS class from requests and limits, a `NodeMemoryPressure` evictor that ranks Pods and evicts in QoS order, and a `VolumeLifecycle` model contrasting emptyDir (lost on reschedule) with a PersistentVolumeClaim (survives). We protect the Transfer Service serving Rajesh and Priya and show the statement cache loss.

Input data: three Pods with different resource settings and a statement cache written to both an emptyDir and a PVC.

Step 1 — The classifier derives each Pod's QoS. The nightly report sets nothing, so it is BestEffort. answers.question: How do you enforce least privilege at the Pod level — `securityContext` with `runAsNonRoot`/`runAsUser`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem`, dropped Linux capabilities, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, and cluster-wide Pod Security Standards/admission (restricted profile) — and why does a container running as root breach "least privilege"?
answers.shortTitle: Enforcing Least Privilege at the Pod Level and Why Running as Root Breaches It

s1_definition.profdef: Least privilege at the Pod level means a container runs with only the permissions it truly needs and nothing more. You enforce it with a securityContext that sets runAsNonRoot and a specific non-zero runAsUser, mounts the root filesystem read-only, drops all Linux capabilities and adds back only the few that are required, and sets allowPrivilegeEscalation to false so a process cannot gain more privileges than it started with. Cluster-wide, Pod Security Admission enforces these rules at admission time using the restricted profile, so non-compliant Pods are rejected. A container running as root breaches least privilege because the root user inside the container maps to a powerful identity that, combined with a kernel or runtime vulnerability, can escalate to control the node.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, least privilege means a junior clerk gets a key that opens only their own drawer, not the vault, the server room, and the CEO's office. The securityContext is the access-control form that says exactly which single drawer this clerk may open, forbids them from carrying tools that pick other locks, and bans them from upgrading their own badge. Pod Security Admission is the security desk at the entrance that refuses to let anyone in who demands master keys. Running as root is like handing every new clerk the building master key on day one, so if any one of them is compromised the attacker owns the whole building.
s1_definition.oneliner: Give a container only the permissions it needs via securityContext, enforce it cluster-wide with the restricted Pod Security profile, and never run as root because root plus one exploit means node takeover.

A container running as root breaches least privilege because the root user inside the container maps to a powerful identity that, combined with a kernel or runtime vulnerability, can escalate to control the node.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, least privilege means a junior clerk gets a key that opens only their own drawer, not the vault, the server room, and the CEO's office. The securityContext is the access-control form that says exactly which single drawer this clerk may open, forbids them from carrying tools that pick other locks, and bans them from upgrading their own badge. Pod Security Admission is the security desk at the entrance that refuses to let anyone in who demands master keys. Running as root is like handing every new clerk the building master key on day one, so if any one of them is compromised the attacker owns the whole building.

sections.s2_technical:
The securityContext is set at the Pod level and can be overridden per container, and several fields together implement least privilege. `runAsNonRoot: true` makes the kubelet refuse to start a container whose image would run as UID 0, which is a safety net. `runAsUser` with a specific non-zero UID, such as 10001, pins the process to an unprivileged account. `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` makes the container's root filesystem immutable, so an attacker cannot drop a malicious binary or tamper with code; the application writes only to explicitly mounted writable volumes like an emptyDir for temporary files.

Linux capabilities are a finer-grained split of root's powers. By default containers get a set of capabilities even as non-root, and least privilege means dropping all of them with `capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]` and adding back only the specific ones a workload genuinely needs, which for a typical banking microservice is none. `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` sets the no-new-privileges flag so a child process cannot gain more privileges than its parent, which blocks setuid-based escalation. Together these shrink the blast radius: even if the application is compromised, the attacker is a non-root user on a read-only filesystem with no capabilities and no way to escalate.

Enforcing this per Pod is good, but relying on every team to remember it is fragile, so Kubernetes provides Pod Security Admission built into the API server. It defines three profiles: privileged (no restrictions), baseline (blocks known privilege escalations), and restricted (the hardened profile that requires runAsNonRoot, dropped capabilities, no privilege escalation, and a restricted seccomp profile). You label a namespace with the profile and a mode: enforce rejects violating Pods, audit records them, and warn returns a warning. For a banking namespace I enforce the restricted profile so any Pod that tries to run as root or request extra capabilities is rejected at admission time, before it ever runs. Many teams layer a policy engine like OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno on top for custom rules such as requiring specific labels or forbidding certain registries.

Why does running as root breach least privilege even inside a container? A container is not a strong security boundary like a virtual machine; it shares the host kernel. Root inside the container is, by default, the same UID 0 the kernel recognizes, so if an attacker escapes the container through a kernel bug, a misconfigured mount, or an added capability like CAP_SYS_ADMIN, they are root on the node and can read every other Pod's secrets, mounted volumes, and the kubelet credentials. Running as an unprivileged user with dropped capabilities and no escalation means that even a successful application compromise is contained to a weak identity that cannot pivot to the node. In a bank, where one node runs many tenants' Pods, that containment is the difference between a single compromised service and a cluster-wide breach.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India a security review of our Transfer Service drove this hardening. Two concrete problems motivated it.

Problem 1 — the base image ran the app as root and the root filesystem was writable, so a code-injection bug could have let an attacker write a malicious binary and, with the default capabilities, probe for a container escape to the node. This is exactly why we set runAsNonRoot, a fixed UID, a read-only root filesystem, dropped all capabilities, and disabled privilege escalation.

Problem 2 — nothing stopped a new team from shipping a Pod that ran as root, so the protection was only as strong as the least careful team. This is exactly why we labelled the namespace with the restricted Pod Security profile in enforce mode, so a root Pod is rejected at admission.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `PodSecurityContext` holding the hardening fields, a `PodSecurityAdmission` that applies the restricted profile and admits or rejects a Pod, and a `BlastRadius` estimator that shows how much an attacker could reach with a root versus a hardened Pod. We admit a hardened Transfer Service that then serves Rajesh and Priya, and reject a root Pod.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one Pod using the insecure defaults (root) and one hardened Pod, both submitted to a namespace enforcing the restricted profile.

Step 1 — The blast-radius estimator looks at the root Pod. It runs as UID 0, allows privilege escalation, and keeps all capabilities, so the estimator reports a HIGH blast radius: a compromise could escape the container and take over the node and every other Pod's secrets.

Step 2 — Admission evaluates the root Pod against the restricted profile. It collects violations: not runAsNonRoot, writable root filesystem, privilege escalation allowed, capabilities not dropped, and an unconfined seccomp profile. Because the list is non-empty, the Pod is rejected before it ever runs.

Step 3 — The blast-radius estimator looks at the hardened Pod. It runs as UID 10001, forbids escalation, and drops all capabilities, so the estimator reports a LOW blast radius: even a full application compromise is contained to a weak identity on a read-only filesystem.

Step 4 — Admission evaluates the hardened Pod. Every requirement is satisfied, so the Pod is admitted.

Step 5 — Because the hardened Pod is admitted and runs, a transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya executes successfully, proving that strong least-privilege settings do not prevent the application from doing its real job.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Least privilege at the Pod level means a container runs with only the permissions it genuinely needs and nothing more, and I implement it through the securityContext. I set runAsNonRoot to true and pin a specific non-zero user ID so the process never runs as root. I mount the root filesystem read-only so an attacker cannot drop a malicious binary or tamper with code, and I give the application a small writable volume only where it truly needs to write. I drop all Linux capabilities and add back only the handful a workload actually requires, which for a typical banking microservice is none. And I set allowPrivilegeEscalation to false so a child process can never gain more privileges than its parent, which blocks setuid-based escalation.

Doing this per Pod is necessary but not sufficient, because relying on every team to remember it is fragile. So cluster-wide I use Pod Security Admission, which is built into the API server and offers privileged, baseline, and restricted profiles. I label the banking namespace with the restricted profile in enforce mode, so any Pod that tries to run as root, keep extra capabilities, or allow escalation is rejected at admission time before it ever runs. For custom organizational rules I layer a policy engine like Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper on top.

The reason running as root breaches least privilege, even inside a container, is that a container is not a strong security boundary the way a virtual machine is; it shares the host kernel. Root inside the container is, by default, the same privileged identity the kernel recognizes, so if an attacker escapes the container through a kernel bug, a bad mount, or a dangerous capability, they become root on the node and can read every other Pod's secrets, mounted volumes, and the node's credentials. Running as an unprivileged user with dropped capabilities and no escalation means that even a full application compromise is contained to a weak identity that cannot pivot to the node.

In my project at the National Bank of India a security review found our Transfer Service running as root with a writable filesystem, which meant a single code-injection bug could have led to a node takeover. We hardened it to run as a fixed unprivileged user on a read-only filesystem with all capabilities dropped and escalation disabled, and crucially we labelled the namespace with the restricted profile in enforce mode so no team could ever ship a root Pod again. The service kept doing its job of moving customers' money exactly as before, but the blast radius of any compromise shrank from the entire cluster to a single weak, contained process, which in a multi-tenant banking cluster is the whole point.

answers.question: What does a container exit code 137 mean (128 + signal 9 = SIGKILL), how do you tell an OOMKill (`kubectl describe pod` → `Reason: OOMKilled`, breached memory limit) from a liveness-probe kill or a manual/graceful-shutdown-timeout kill, and how do you fix each (right-size limits + container-aware JVM `MaxRAMPercentage`, fix the leak, or tune probe/termination grace)?
answers.shortTitle: What Exit Code 137 Means, and Telling OOMKill from Liveness-Probe Kill from Graceful-Shutdown Timeout

s1_definition.profdef: Exit code 137 means a process was terminated by signal 9, SIGKILL, because Linux encodes signal termination as 128 plus the signal number. In Kubernetes a 137 can come from several distinct causes that all end in SIGKILL: the kernel out-of-memory killer when a container breaches its memory limit, the kubelet killing a container whose liveness probe failed, or the kubelet force-killing a container that did not exit within its termination grace period after a graceful shutdown request. You distinguish them from the Pod's describe output and events: OOMKilled shows Reason OOMKilled, a liveness kill shows unhealthy liveness events before the restart, and a grace-timeout kill shows a preceding SIGTERM and a kill after the grace window.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, exit code 137 is like a security guard physically carrying a teller out of the building — it only tells you the teller was removed by force, not why. Maybe they overflowed their cubicle with files (OOMKill), maybe the manager kept knocking and got no answer so declared them unresponsive (liveness kill), or maybe closing time came, they were asked politely to leave, they dawdled past the deadline, and the guard removed them (graceful-shutdown timeout). The forced removal looks identical; you read the incident log to learn the real reason and fix the right thing.
s1_definition.oneliner: 137 is SIGKILL (128 plus 9) and only says "force-killed"; read describe and events to tell OOMKill from a liveness-probe kill from a grace-timeout kill, then fix memory, probe, or shutdown respectively.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Exit code 137 means a process was terminated by signal 9, SIGKILL, because Linux encodes signal termination as 128 plus the signal number. In Kubernetes a 137 can come from several distinct causes that all end in SIGKILL: the kernel out-of-memory killer when a container breaches its memory limit, the kubelet killing a container whose liveness probe failed, or the kubelet force-killing a container that did not exit within its termination grace period after a graceful shutdown request. You distinguish them from the Pod's describe output and events: OOMKilled shows Reason OOMKilled, a liveness kill shows unhealthy liveness events before the restart, and a grace-timeout kill shows a preceding SIGTERM and a kill after the grace window.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, exit code 137 is like a security guard physically carrying a teller out of the building — it only tells you the teller was removed by force, not why. Maybe they overflowed their cubicle with files (OOMKill), maybe the manager kept knocking and got no answer so declared them unresponsive (liveness kill), or maybe closing time came, they were asked politely to leave, they dawdled past the deadline, and the guard removed them (graceful-shutdown timeout). The forced removal looks identical; you read the incident log to learn the real reason and fix the right thing.

**One line to remember:** 137 is SIGKILL (128 plus 9) and only says "force-killed"; read describe and events to tell OOMKill from a liveness-probe kill from a grace-timeout kill, then fix memory, probe, or shutdown respectively.

sections.s2_technical:
The number itself decodes cleanly. When a process is terminated by a signal, the shell and container runtime report the exit status as 128 plus the signal number. Signal 9 is SIGKILL, so 128 plus 9 is 137. SIGKILL cannot be caught or handled, so the process dies immediately with no chance to clean up. Importantly, 137 is a symptom shared by several causes, so the number alone never tells you what to fix.

The first cause is an OOMKill. When a container exceeds its cgroup memory limit, the kernel's out-of-memory killer sends SIGKILL. You identify this in `kubectl describe pod` under the container's Last State, where Reason shows OOMKilled and the exit code is 137. The fix is about memory: right-size the memory limit above the real peak of total process memory, make the JVM container-aware by setting the maximum heap as a percentage of the limit so it leaves room for off-heap and native memory, and if the limit already looks generous, hunt for a memory leak because a steadily climbing working set that always ends in OOMKilled is a leak, not an undersizing.

The second cause is a liveness-probe kill. If the liveness probe fails past its failure threshold, the kubelet kills the container to restart it, and that kill is a SIGKILL after a grace period, so it too surfaces as 137. You tell this apart because `kubectl describe pod` and the events show "Liveness probe failed" messages and a Killing event citing the failed probe immediately before the restart, and the restart count climbs in lockstep with probe failures rather than with memory. The fix is about the probe and the app: if the probe is too aggressive or points at a path that depends on a slow downstream, loosen the threshold or timeout and make the liveness endpoint a trivial self-check; if the app genuinely hangs, fix the hang such as a deadlock or a blocked thread pool.

The third cause is a graceful-shutdown timeout. When a Pod is deleted or rescheduled, the kubelet sends SIGTERM and waits up to terminationGracePeriodSeconds for the process to exit cleanly; if it does not exit in time, the kubelet sends SIGKILL, which is 137. You recognize this because the events show the Pod being terminated with a SIGTERM first and then a kill after the grace window, and it happens during deploys, scale-downs, or evictions rather than randomly. The fix is about shutdown: make the application handle SIGTERM by stopping intake, draining in-flight work, and exiting within the grace period, and if clean shutdown legitimately takes longer, raise terminationGracePeriodSeconds and add a preStop hook to delay for connection draining. A senior nuance is that a too-short grace period in a banking service can cut off in-flight transfers mid-commit, so I size the grace period to the longest safe in-flight operation and ensure the app actually listens for SIGTERM, which a JVM does through a shutdown hook. The disciplined method across all three is identical: never act on the 137 alone, always open describe, read the Last State reason and the events timeline, and only then apply the memory fix, the probe fix, or the shutdown fix.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India our Transfer Service showed exit code 137 on three different days with three different root causes, which is why we built a decision procedure instead of guessing.

Problem 1 — one day the restart count climbed with memory usage and describe showed Reason OOMKilled, so the fix was memory sizing and a container-aware heap.

Problem 2 — another day the restarts tracked liveness failures because the probe called a path that waited on a slow database, so the fix was a trivial liveness endpoint and a looser threshold.

Problem 3 — a third day the 137s only appeared during deploys because the service took forty seconds to drain in-flight transfers but the grace period was thirty, so the fix was a longer grace period plus a proper SIGTERM handler.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `KillClassifier` that takes the evidence a real describe would show and classifies the 137 as OOMKILL, LIVENESS_KILL, or GRACE_TIMEOUT, then prints the correct fix. A `GracefulShutdown` class models a JVM shutdown hook draining a transfer for Rajesh and Priya within the grace window versus being SIGKILLed when it overruns.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three sets of describe evidence all showing exit code 137, plus two shutdown scenarios.

Step 1 — Day 1 evidence shows exit code 137 with Last State Reason OOMKilled. The classifier first notes that 137 is 128 plus signal 9, then sees the OOMKilled reason and classifies it as an OOMKill, prescribing memory right-sizing and a container-aware heap.

Step 2 — Day 2 evidence shows 137 with a generic Error reason but a liveness-probe-failed flag set before the restart. The classifier rules out OOM because the reason is not OOMKilled, sees the liveness failures, and classifies it as a liveness kill, prescribing a trivial liveness endpoint and a looser threshold.

Step 3 — Day 3 evidence shows 137 with a SIGTERM-then-kill flag and the kill happening during a deploy. The classifier rules out OOM and liveness, sees the SIGTERM-then-kill during a deploy, and classifies it as a graceful-shutdown timeout, prescribing a longer grace period and a SIGTERM drain handler.

Step 4 — The graceful-shutdown model is tested with a drain that needs forty seconds but a grace period of only thirty. The drain overruns, so the process is SIGKILLed with exit 137 and the in-flight transfer is cut off, reproducing Day 3's failure.

Step 5 — The grace period is raised to sixty seconds while the drain needs only twenty. On SIGTERM the service stops intake, drains, commits the transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya cleanly, and exits with code 0, proving the fix.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Exit code 137 decodes as 128 plus signal 9, which is SIGKILL, so the number tells me only that the process was force-killed and had no chance to clean up. The crucial point I always make is that 137 is a symptom shared by several different causes, so I never act on the number alone. I open the Pod's describe output and the events timeline first, because that is what reveals the actual reason.

The first possible cause is an out-of-memory kill, where the container breached its cgroup memory limit and the kernel sent SIGKILL. I identify it by the Last State reason showing OOMKilled alongside the 137. The fix is about memory: I right-size the memory limit above the real peak of total process memory, I make the JVM container-aware by setting the maximum heap as a percentage of the limit so it leaves headroom for off-heap and native memory, and if the limit already looks generous but the working set keeps climbing to the kill, I treat it as a leak and profile it rather than just raising the limit.

The second cause is a liveness-probe kill, where the probe failed past its threshold and the kubelet restarted the container, which also surfaces as 137. I tell it apart because the events show liveness-probe-failed messages and a killing event citing the probe right before the restart, and the restart count tracks probe failures rather than memory. The fix is to make the liveness endpoint a trivial self-check rather than something that depends on a slow downstream, loosen an overly aggressive threshold or timeout, and if the application genuinely hangs, fix the underlying deadlock. The third cause is a graceful-shutdown timeout, where the kubelet sent SIGTERM during a deploy or eviction and then SIGKILLed the container because it did not exit within the termination grace period. I recognize it because the events show SIGTERM followed by a kill after the grace window, and it happens during deploys rather than at random. The fix is to handle SIGTERM by stopping intake and draining in-flight work, raise the grace period to cover the longest safe operation, and add a preStop hook so the load balancer stops sending traffic before shutdown begins.

In my project at the National Bank of India our Transfer Service threw a 137 on three different days with three different root causes: one was a genuine OOMKill fixed by memory sizing, one was a liveness probe pointing at a slow database path fixed by a trivial liveness endpoint, and one only appeared during deploys because our drain needed forty seconds but the grace period was thirty, which was cutting in-flight transfers off mid-commit. That last one was the most dangerous in a bank, so we raised the grace period beyond the worst-case drain and added a proper SIGTERM handler through a JVM shutdown hook. The lesson I carry is that the exit code is where the investigation starts, never where it ends, and the right fix depends entirely on reading the reason behind the SIGKILL.

answers.question: (Scenario) An EKS cluster is slow but CPU and memory look NORMAL — how do you troubleshoot across the whole request path rather than one dashboard (Application: latency/error rate/thread & connection pools/downstream DB latency; Kubernetes: pod scheduling/restarts/events/probe failures/pending pods; Node: disk I/O, network, disk pressure, kernel, container runtime; Networking: CoreDNS/DNS latency, service-to-service, NetworkPolicy, LB; Control plane: API-server latency, etcd) — and why are CPU/memory only two of many signals?
answers.shortTitle: (Scenario) An EKS Cluster Is Slow but CPU and Memory Look Normal

s1_definition.profdef: When an EKS cluster is slow but CPU and memory look normal, the bottleneck is on a dimension those two metrics do not capture, so you troubleshoot the whole request path across five layers: the application (latency, error rate, thread and connection pool saturation, downstream database latency), Kubernetes (scheduling delays, restarts, events, probe failures, pending Pods), the node (disk input-output, network throughput, disk pressure, kernel, container runtime), networking (CoreDNS and DNS latency, service-to-service calls, NetworkPolicy, load balancer health), and the control plane (API server latency, etcd health). CPU and memory are only two signals because latency is usually caused by waiting rather than computing, such as a saturated connection pool, slow DNS, or a slow downstream, none of which raise CPU.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India the branch is slow but every teller looks relaxed and the lights are not dimming, so it is not a staffing or power problem. The real delay could be that there is only one phone line to the vault and everyone is queued on it (connection pool), the directory assistance desk is slow to look up extensions (DNS), the central records office in another city is slow to answer (downstream database), or the building's front-gate turnstile is jammed (load balancer). You would never find any of these by only watching how hard the tellers are working, so you walk the entire customer journey end to end.

sections.s2_technical:
The reason CPU and memory mislead is that most latency comes from blocking on a resource, not from burning cycles. A request thread that is parked waiting for a database connection, a DNS answer, or a downstream response consumes almost no CPU while the user waits seconds. So the first discipline is to stop staring at the two easy dashboards and instead follow the request through every layer.

At the application layer I look at request latency percentiles and error rate, and crucially at pool saturation. A thread pool that is exhausted or a database connection pool like HikariCP that is at its maximum will queue requests, so I check active-versus-max connections and the pool wait time. I also measure downstream database query latency directly, because a slow query plan or a lock contention in the database shows up as app slowness with flat app CPU. Distributed tracing is the best tool here because it attributes the time to the exact hop that is slow.

At the Kubernetes layer I check for scheduling delays and pending Pods, restart counts, and probe failures, because a Pod that keeps failing readiness is quietly removed from the Service and concentrates load on fewer Pods, which raises latency without raising average CPU. Events often reveal evictions or image pull delays. At the node layer I look at disk input-output and disk pressure, network saturation, kernel issues, and the container runtime, because a node with saturated disk or network, or under disk pressure, slows every Pod on it even though CPU and memory read normal. Noisy neighbors and throttling live here.

At the networking layer, DNS is the classic hidden cause: if CoreDNS is overloaded or misconfigured, every outbound call pays a DNS penalty of tens or hundreds of milliseconds, which compounds across microservice hops. I check CoreDNS latency and error rate, service-to-service call latency, whether a NetworkPolicy is forcing retries, and load balancer health and connection limits. At the control plane layer, which in EKS is managed by AWS but still observable, a slow API server or unhealthy etcd makes controllers, scheduling, and any in-cluster client that calls the API slow, so I check API server request latency and throttling. The senior point is that CPU and memory are just two of a dozen signals, and latency debugging is fundamentally about finding where time is spent waiting, which means correlating traces, pool metrics, DNS metrics, node input-output, and control-plane latency rather than trusting a single green dashboard.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India our Transfer Service got slow one afternoon, yet CPU and memory were a calm forty percent, which is exactly the trap this question describes. The scenario reproduces the end-to-end hunt.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer traced while CPU reads a normal forty percent, first slow and then after fixes.

Step 1 — The slow trace runs with CPU at forty percent, which looks healthy. The connection pool is set to ten active out of ten maximum, so it is saturated, and CoreDNS latency is set to three hundred milliseconds because of a DNS spike.

Step 2 — The tracer attributes the total time across spans: forty milliseconds of application compute, three hundred milliseconds of DNS resolution, two thousand five hundred milliseconds of pool wait because the pool is saturated, and sixty milliseconds of database query. The total is two thousand nine hundred milliseconds, far above the target, while CPU stayed normal.

Step 3 — The tracer identifies the biggest span, the pool wait, as the bottleneck and reports that it is waiting rather than CPU, also flagging the elevated DNS latency. This is exactly the real-world finding: the time is spent blocking, not computing.

Step 4 — We apply the fixes by enlarging the connection pool so it has headroom at twelve active out of thirty, and by fixing CoreDNS so DNS latency drops back to three milliseconds.

Step 5 — The tracer re-runs with the same normal CPU. Now the pool wait is five milliseconds and DNS is three milliseconds, so the total falls to roughly one hundred milliseconds. The transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya completes fast, proving that the fix targeted the real waiting bottleneck rather than adding compute.

sections.s6_takeaway:
When a cluster is slow but CPU and memory look normal, I immediately stop trusting those two dashboards, because latency is almost always about time spent waiting rather than time spent computing. A request thread parked on a saturated connection pool, a slow DNS lookup, or a slow downstream call consumes almost no CPU while the user waits seconds, so a green CPU graph is expected and tells me nothing about the real problem. CPU and memory are just two signals among a dozen.

So I troubleshoot the whole request path across five layers. At the application layer I look at latency percentiles, error rate, and especially pool saturation, checking active-versus-maximum connections and pool wait time, and I measure downstream database query latency directly, with distributed tracing attributing time to the exact slow hop. At the Kubernetes layer I check for pending Pods, restarts, probe failures, and events, because a Pod failing readiness is quietly pulled from the Service and concentrates load on fewer Pods. At the node layer I check disk input-output, disk pressure, network saturation, and the container runtime, because a saturated or pressured node slows every Pod on it with normal CPU. At the networking layer I treat DNS as a prime suspect, because an overloaded CoreDNS adds a penalty to every outbound call that compounds across microservice hops, and I also check service-to-service latency, NetworkPolicy-induced retries, and load balancer health. At the control plane layer I check API server and etcd latency, because a slow control plane slows scheduling and any in-cluster client.

The reason this breadth matters is that the wrong instinct, adding more Pods because the system is slow, wastes money and fixes nothing when the bottleneck is a connection pool or DNS. In my project at the National Bank of India our Transfer Service suddenly took three seconds instead of a hundred milliseconds while CPU sat at a calm forty percent. Tracing showed the time was spent waiting on a saturated HikariCP pool, and separately CoreDNS latency had spiked and was taxing every downstream call. Neither would ever appear on a CPU graph. Enlarging the connection pool so it had headroom and fixing the CoreDNS issue brought latency back to around a hundred milliseconds. The lesson I carry is that latency debugging is about finding where time is spent waiting, which means correlating traces, pool metrics, DNS metrics, node input-output, and control-plane latency across the entire path rather than concluding everything is fine because two dashboards are green.

answers.question: How does EKS consume VPC IP addresses so quickly (the VPC CNI assigns real VPC IPs to pods), what causes IP exhaustion, and how do you fix/avoid it (add subnets / associate a secondary VPC CIDR, review pod density, prefix delegation, consider IPv6, and monitor IP utilization proactively BEFORE production scale)?
answers.shortTitle: Why EKS Consumes VPC IP Addresses So Quickly, and How to Avoid IP Exhaustion

s1_definition.profdef: In Amazon EKS the default Amazon VPC CNI plugin gives every Pod a real, routable IP address from the VPC subnet rather than an overlay address, so each Pod consumes one usable subnet IP just like an EC2 instance does. Because subnets have a finite IP range and the CNI also pre-allocates warm IPs to each node for fast Pod startup, IP addresses are consumed far faster than Pod count alone suggests. IP exhaustion happens when the subnets run out of free addresses, which blocks new Pods from starting. You avoid it by adding subnets or a secondary VPC CIDR, reducing per-node warm-IP over-allocation, enabling prefix delegation to pack more Pods per ENI, considering IPv6, and monitoring IP utilization before you hit production scale.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India every new teller, instead of sharing a single branch phone line, gets their own direct outside phone number from the city's limited pool. That is wonderful for reaching them directly, but the city only has so many numbers, and the phone company even reserves a block of spare numbers per department in advance so new tellers can start instantly. So the pool drains much faster than the headcount suggests, and one day a new teller cannot start because there are no numbers left. The fix is to get more number ranges allocated, reserve fewer spares per department, or move to a vastly larger numbering scheme.
s1_definition.oneliner: EKS gives each Pod a real VPC IP and pre-warms spare IPs per node, so subnets drain fast; avoid exhaustion with more CIDR space, prefix delegation, IPv6, and proactive IP-utilization monitoring.
