sections.s2_technical:
The Amazon VPC CNI is what makes EKS networking fast and native: because Pods get real VPC IPs, they are reachable directly, security groups and VPC flow logs work naturally, and there is no overlay encapsulation overhead. The cost of that design is IP consumption. Each worker node attaches elastic network interfaces, and each interface can hold a limited number of secondary IPs depending on the instance type. The CNI assigns Pod IPs from those secondary IPs, so the number of Pods a node can run is bounded by how many IPs its interfaces can hold.

The consumption is faster than it looks for two reasons. First, the CNI maintains a warm pool: to start Pods quickly it pre-allocates spare IPs on each node ahead of demand, so a node running ten Pods may be holding twenty or thirty reserved IPs. Multiply that across many nodes and a large fraction of the subnet is reserved but not actively used. Second, Pod churn from frequent deploys constantly cycles IPs, and IPs are not always released instantly, so transient consumption spikes during rollouts.

IP exhaustion is when the subnets backing the node group run out of free addresses. The symptom is new Pods stuck in ContainerCreating with CNI errors about failing to assign an IP, and nodes that cannot schedule more Pods even though they have spare CPU and memory. This is a capacity-planning failure, not a code bug, and it tends to bite exactly when you scale toward production because that is when Pod and node counts climb.

The fixes form a toolkit. The simplest is to give the VPC more room by adding larger or additional subnets, or associating a secondary CIDR block with the VPC and running node groups there, which immediately enlarges the address pool. I tune the warm-pool behavior with the CNI environment variables that control how many spare IPs each node pre-allocates, trading slightly slower Pod startup for far less reservation waste. The most impactful fix on IPv4 is prefix delegation, where instead of assigning individual secondary IPs the CNI assigns each interface a slash-twenty-eight prefix of sixteen addresses, dramatically increasing how many Pods a node supports and reducing API churn. For a genuinely large platform the strategic answer is IPv6, where the address space is effectively unlimited and exhaustion stops being a concern. The non-negotiable practice is proactive monitoring: I watch subnet free-IP counts and the CNI's available-IP metric and alert well before utilization gets high, because the right time to discover an IP shortage is during capacity planning, not when a production deploy stalls. The senior point is that this is a design consequence of the native-IP model, so it must be planned at VPC design time, not patched under pressure.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India our EKS platform grew from a pilot to production, and IP exhaustion nearly caused an outage, which is why this is a real lesson rather than a theoretical one.

Problem 1 — during a scale-up for a festive-season load test, new Transfer Service Pods got stuck in ContainerCreating with CNI "failed to assign IP" errors, even though nodes had plenty of CPU and memory. The small pilot subnet had run out of addresses because the CNI warm pool had reserved most of them. This is exactly subnet exhaustion from native-IP plus warm-pool reservation.

Problem 2 — we needed a durable fix, not just a one-time subnet bump, because growth would continue. This is exactly why we associated a secondary CIDR, enabled prefix delegation to pack far more Pods per node, and added proactive alerting on subnet free IPs.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `VpcSubnet` with a finite IP pool, a `VpcCni` that assigns Pod IPs and maintains a warm pool, and an `IpCapacityPlanner` that reports utilization, raises an alert before exhaustion, and shows how prefix delegation and a secondary CIDR expand capacity. We try to schedule Transfer Service Pods serving Rajesh and Priya, hit exhaustion, then apply the fixes and succeed.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a small pilot subnet with twenty-seven usable IPs and a warm pool of fourteen per node, then a fix with a large secondary CIDR and prefix delegation.

Step 1 — The first node starts with ten Pods. The CNI reserves the ten Pod IPs plus fourteen warm spares, which is twenty-four IPs from the twenty-seven-address subnet. The planner reports utilization near eighty-nine percent and raises the proactive alert.

Step 2 — A second node tries to start with another ten Pods, needing twenty-four more IPs, but only three are free. The subnet is exhausted, so the allocation fails and the new Pods are stuck in ContainerCreating with a CNI "failed to assign IP" error, even though the nodes have spare CPU and memory.

Step 3 — We apply the durable fix by associating a large secondary CIDR with roughly a thousand usable IPs for the node groups, which immediately enlarges the pool.

Step 4 — We enable prefix delegation so the CNI assigns slash-twenty-eight prefixes of sixteen IPs per slot, and we shrink the warm pool to two spares per node, so reservation waste drops sharply.

Step 5 — Three nodes each start with thirty Pods and allocate successfully from the large pool. The planner reports a low utilization well under the alert threshold. A transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya runs successfully because the Pods now have IPs, proving the fix scaled the platform safely.

And the non-negotiable practice is proactive monitoring of subnet free IPs and the CNI's available-IP metric, with alerts well before utilization gets high.

In my project at the National Bank of India this nearly caused an outage. During a festive-season scale-up, new Transfer Service Pods got stuck in ContainerCreating with IP-assignment errors because our small pilot subnet had run out of addresses, mostly consumed by the warm pool, even though the nodes had plenty of compute. We fixed it durably by associating a large secondary CIDR, enabling prefix delegation to pack far more Pods per node, shrinking the warm pool, and adding an alert at eighty percent subnet utilization. The lesson I always emphasize is that this is a design consequence of the native-IP model, so IP capacity must be planned at VPC-design time and watched proactively, because the worst possible moment to discover an IP shortage is when a production deploy stalls under load.

---

answers.question: What is Terraform, what is the Terraform state file, why does it matter, and how do you manage remote state (S3 + DynamoDB lock / Terraform Cloud) with state locking to prevent concurrent-apply conflicts?
answers.shortTitle: Terraform, the State File, and Managing Remote State with Locking

s1_definition.profdef: Terraform is an infrastructure-as-code tool that lets you declare cloud resources in configuration files and provisions them to match. The Terraform state file is a JSON record that maps the resources declared in your configuration to the real resources that exist in the cloud, storing their identifiers and attributes. It matters because Terraform diffs the desired configuration against the state to compute what to create, change, or destroy. Remote state stores that file in a shared backend such as an S3 bucket, and state locking, using DynamoDB with the S3 backend or built into Terraform Cloud, ensures only one apply runs at a time so concurrent applies cannot corrupt the state.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Terraform is like a master plan that says exactly how the branch should be built: three counters, one vault, two ATMs. The state file is the branch's official inventory ledger recording which specific vault and which specific ATMs were actually installed, by serial number. The plan on its own does not know what already exists; it consults the ledger. Remote state keeps that single ledger in the head office safe so every engineer reads the same copy, and state locking is the rule that only one person may write in the ledger at a time, so two engineers cannot both renovate the branch simultaneously and leave the ledger contradicting reality.
s1_definition.oneliner: Terraform declares infrastructure, the state file maps config to real resources, and remote state with locking keeps a single shared, uncorrupted source of truth so concurrent applies cannot clash.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Terraform is an infrastructure-as-code tool that lets you declare cloud resources in configuration files and provisions them to match. The Terraform state file is a JSON record that maps the resources declared in your configuration to the real resources that exist in the cloud, storing their identifiers and attributes. It matters because Terraform diffs the desired configuration against the state to compute what to create, change, or destroy. Remote state stores that file in a shared backend such as an S3 bucket, and state locking, using DynamoDB with the S3 backend or built into Terraform Cloud, ensures only one apply runs at a time so concurrent applies cannot corrupt the state.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Terraform is like a master plan that says exactly how the branch should be built: three counters, one vault, two ATMs. The state file is the branch's official inventory ledger recording which specific vault and which specific ATMs were actually installed, by serial number. The plan on its own does not know what already exists; it consults the ledger. Remote state keeps that single ledger in the head office safe so every engineer reads the same copy, and state locking is the rule that only one person may write in the ledger at a time, so two engineers cannot both renovate the branch simultaneously and leave the ledger contradicting reality.

**One line to remember:** Terraform declares infrastructure, the state file maps config to real resources, and remote state with locking keeps a single shared, uncorrupted source of truth so concurrent applies cannot clash.

sections.s2_technical:
Terraform works declaratively: you write configuration describing the desired end state, Terraform reads the current state file, queries the providers for reality, and produces a plan of the minimal changes needed to reconcile the two. Then apply executes that plan and updates the state. Without the state file, Terraform would have no memory of what it created and could not tell the difference between a resource it should update and one it should create fresh, so the state is the backbone of the whole workflow.

The state file stores more than names. It holds resource identifiers like an instance ID or an ARN, attribute values, dependency ordering, and sometimes sensitive outputs, which is exactly why it must be protected. A state file can contain secrets such as a generated database password, so it should never be committed to Git and should be encrypted at rest. This is the first reason remote state matters: a local state file on one engineer's laptop is unshared, unencrypted, and easily lost.

Remote state puts the file in a shared backend so the whole team and the CI pipeline read and write the same authoritative copy. With the S3 backend, the state lives in a versioned, encrypted S3 bucket. Versioning is important because it keeps historical copies, so a corrupted or accidentally truncated state can be rolled back to a previous version. The configuration points Terraform at the bucket, key, and region.

State locking prevents the most dangerous failure mode: two applies running at once. If two engineers or two pipeline runs apply simultaneously against the same state, they can read the same starting state, make conflicting changes, and write back a state that no longer matches reality, which can orphan or duplicate resources. With the S3 backend you add a DynamoDB table for locking: before an apply, Terraform writes a lock item to the table, and any second apply that sees the lock waits or fails fast with a clear message rather than racing. Terraform Cloud and other managed backends provide equivalent locking built in, plus run queuing so applies are serialized automatically. The senior discipline in a bank is to always use remote state with locking and versioning, restrict who can read the state because it holds secrets, and run applies through a controlled pipeline so that the lock, the plan review, and the audit trail are consistent. I also keep separate state files per environment so a mistake in dev can never touch production state.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India our platform team manages the EKS cluster, VPC, and databases with Terraform. Two real problems shaped how we handle state.

Problem 1 — early on, state lived locally on one engineer's laptop. When that engineer was on leave and someone else ran an apply from a fresh checkout, Terraform did not know the resources already existed and tried to create duplicates, nearly provisioning a second production database. This is exactly why state must be shared and remote.

Problem 2 — once state was in S3, two pipeline runs triggered by two merges applied at nearly the same time and raced on the state, leaving it inconsistent. This is exactly why we added DynamoDB locking so only one apply proceeds and the other waits.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `TerraformState` holding resource mappings, a `S3StateBackend` that stores versioned state, and a `DynamoLock` that serializes applies. An `ApplyRunner` performs a plan-and-apply that provisions the banking infrastructure, and we demonstrate a second concurrent apply being blocked by the lock. The `Account` model ties the provisioned database to a working transfer for Rajesh and Priya.

```
├── sim/src/main/java/com/bank/tf/

│   ├── Account.java
│   ├── TerraformState.java       (config→real resource map)
│   ├── S3StateBackend.java       (versioned remote state)
│   ├── DynamoLock.java           (serialize applies)
│   ├── ApplyRunner.java          (plan + apply under lock)
│   └── BankLogFormatter.java
```

##### 4c. Terraform backend configuration

```hcl
# backend.tf — remote state in S3 with DynamoDB locking + encryption + versioning
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket         = "nbi-terraform-state"
    key            = "prod/eks/terraform.tfstate"   # separate key per environment
    region         = "ap-south-1"
    dynamodb_table = "nbi-terraform-locks"           # state locking
    encrypt        = true                            # encrypt state at rest
  }
}
```

```bash
# Real Terraform with remote state + locking

terraform plan          # diff config vs state, show changes
terraform apply         # acquires DynamoDB lock, applies, updates S3 state
terraform state list    # inspect tracked resources
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a desired infrastructure list of a VPC, an EKS cluster, and a ledger database, applied twice and then raced.

Step 1 — The first apply by pipeline-run-1 acquires the DynamoDB lock, loads an empty state, and for each resource sees it is missing, so it creates it and records a real ID in the state. The S3 backend saves version one of the state, encrypted, and the lock is released.

Step 2 — A second apply by pipeline-run-2, simulating a fresh checkout by another engineer, acquires the lock and loads the saved state. This time every resource is already present in the state, so the plan reports no changes and no duplicates are created. This is exactly the duplicate-database disaster that shared remote state prevents.

Step 3 — To show locking, a long-running apply takes the lock. A racing apply then tries to acquire it, sees the lock is held, and is blocked with a clear message to wait, rather than racing and corrupting the state.

Step 4 — The long-running apply releases the lock, after which applies could proceed again in a serialized order.

Step 5 — Because the ledger database was provisioned exactly once and tracked in state, it backs a real transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya, which succeeds, tying the infrastructure correctness back to a working banking operation.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Terraform is an infrastructure-as-code tool where I declare the desired end state of my cloud resources and Terraform provisions reality to match. The engine of that workflow is the state file, which is a JSON record mapping every resource in my configuration to the real resource that exists in the cloud, storing its identifiers and attributes. It matters because Terraform computes changes by diffing the desired configuration against the state and then against reality, so without the state Terraform would have no memory of what it created and could not tell an update apart from a brand-new creation.

Because the state is so central, how I store it is a first-order decision. A local state file on one laptop is unshared, unencrypted, and easily lost, and worse, state can contain secrets like a generated database password, so it must never be committed to Git. The answer is remote state in a shared backend. With the S3 backend the state lives in a versioned, encrypted bucket so the whole team and the CI pipeline read and write the same authoritative copy, and versioning lets me roll back to a previous state if a write corrupts it.

The most dangerous failure mode is two applies running at once, because they can read the same starting state, make conflicting changes, and write back a state that no longer matches reality, orphaning or duplicating resources. State locking prevents that. With the S3 backend I add a DynamoDB table, and before an apply Terraform writes a lock item so any second apply waits or fails fast with a clear message instead of racing. Terraform Cloud provides equivalent locking and run queuing built in. Alongside locking I keep separate state per environment so a mistake in dev can never touch production, and I restrict who can read the state because it holds secrets.

In my project at the National Bank of India both lessons came from real incidents. Early on, state lived on one engineer's laptop, and when someone else applied from a fresh checkout Terraform did not know the resources existed and nearly created a duplicate production database. Moving the state to a versioned, encrypted S3 bucket fixed that by giving everyone one shared source of truth. Then two pipeline runs applied almost simultaneously and raced on the state, so we added a DynamoDB lock table that serializes applies and blocks the second one until the first finishes. Together, remote state with versioning and locking turned our Terraform workflow from a fragile, laptop-bound process into a safe, auditable one that reliably provisions the very infrastructure our transfers run on.

answers.question: What are Terraform modules and workspaces, and how do you structure reusable modules for multiple environments (dev/staging/prod)?
answers.shortTitle: Terraform Modules and Workspaces, and Structuring Reusable Modules for Multiple Environments

s1_definition.profdef: A Terraform module is a reusable, parameterized container of resources defined once and instantiated many times with different input variables, which keeps infrastructure code DRY. A workspace is a named instance of a single configuration's state, letting the same configuration hold multiple independent state copies. For multiple environments the robust pattern is reusable modules composed from a thin per-environment root configuration, each environment having its own backend state and its own variable values, rather than relying on workspaces alone to separate production from development.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India a module is the standard blueprint for a branch: you design the counters, vault, and ATMs once, then stamp out a small branch in one town and a large branch in another by just changing the inputs like counter count and vault size. A workspace is like keeping separate inventory ledgers for the same blueprint, so the test branch and the real branch each have their own records. The strongest setup gives each real environment its own blueprint instantiation and its own locked ledger, so a renovation in the test branch can never accidentally touch the main branch.
s1_definition.oneliner: Modules are reusable parameterized infrastructure blueprints, workspaces are named state copies of one configuration, and the safest multi-environment layout composes shared modules from thin per-environment roots with separate state.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Terraform module is a reusable, parameterized container of resources defined once and instantiated many times with different input variables, which keeps infrastructure code DRY. A workspace is a named instance of a single configuration's state, letting the same configuration hold multiple independent state copies. For multiple environments the robust pattern is reusable modules composed from a thin per-environment root configuration, each environment having its own backend state and its own variable values, rather than relying on workspaces alone to separate production from development.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India a module is the standard blueprint for a branch: you design the counters, vault, and ATMs once, then stamp out a small branch in one town and a large branch in another by just changing the inputs like counter count and vault size. A workspace is like keeping separate inventory ledgers for the same blueprint, so the test branch and the real branch each have their own records. The strongest setup gives each real environment its own blueprint instantiation and its own locked ledger, so a renovation in the test branch can never accidentally touch the main branch.

**One line to remember:** Modules are reusable parameterized infrastructure blueprints, workspaces are named state copies of one configuration, and the safest multi-environment layout composes shared modules from thin per-environment roots with separate state.

sections.s2_technical:
A module is simply a directory of Terraform files with input variables, resources, and output values. The root configuration is itself a module, and it calls child modules with a module block that passes inputs. The power is reuse: I write a network module once that creates a VPC, subnets, and routing, then call it from dev with a small CIDR and from production with a large CIDR, so the logic is identical and only the inputs differ. Modules expose outputs so callers can wire one module's results into another, for example passing the VPC module's subnet IDs into an EKS module.

Good module design follows clear rules. Inputs are declared as typed variables with descriptions and sensible defaults where appropriate, outputs expose exactly what callers need, and the module does one coherent job such as networking or a database. Modules are versioned when published to a registry so a caller pins a specific version, which gives reproducible builds. This mirrors writing a well-encapsulated function: clear parameters, a single responsibility, and a clear return.

A workspace is a named state within a single backend for one configuration. Running terraform workspace new dev creates a separate state file keyed by workspace, so the same configuration can manage dev and prod state independently, and you can branch behavior on terraform.workspace. Workspaces are lightweight and good for ephemeral or very similar variants, such as per-developer sandboxes or short-lived feature stacks. However, there are real cautions for production. All workspaces of a configuration share the same backend and the same configuration code, so a change to the configuration affects every workspace, and it is easy to run a command against the wrong workspace and hit production by accident. For that reason many teams, including in regulated banking, do not use workspaces to separate production from lower environments.

The recommended structure for dev, staging, and production is a composition pattern. I keep the reusable logic in a modules directory with modules like network, eks, and database. Then I create a thin root per environment, each with its own backend configuration pointing at a separate state key, its own variable values file, and module blocks that call the shared modules with environment-appropriate inputs. Production might call the eks module with ten nodes and a large instance type while dev calls it with two small nodes, all from the same module code. This gives strong isolation because each environment has its own locked, versioned state and its own blast radius, while the shared modules guarantee the environments stay structurally consistent and do not drift apart. The senior point is that modules deliver reuse and consistency, workspaces deliver lightweight state variants, and for serious multi-environment separation I compose shared modules from per-environment roots with isolated state rather than leaning on workspaces for the prod boundary.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India our platform spans dev, staging, and production, and this structure came directly from two problems.

Problem 1 — we used to copy the full EKS and network configuration into three folders, and they drifted, so staging and production ended up with subtly different cluster settings and a bug slipped through that staging could not reproduce. This is exactly what shared modules fix: one module, three callers, no drift.

Problem 2 — someone once ran an apply against the wrong workspace and nearly changed production while intending dev. This is exactly why we moved the production boundary to separate per-environment roots with isolated state instead of relying on workspace selection.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `Module` abstraction that takes inputs and produces resources, an `EnvironmentRoot` that composes the network and EKS modules with per-environment inputs and its own state key, and a `Workspace` concept shown for lightweight variants. We instantiate dev and production from the same module code and run a transfer for Rajesh and Priya on the production cluster to tie it together.

```
bank-infra/
├── modules/
│   ├── network/   (main.tf, variables.tf, outputs.tf)
│   └── eks/       (main.tf, variables.tf, outputs.tf)
├── envs/
│   ├── dev/       (main.tf, backend.tf, dev.tfvars)
│   ├── staging/   (main.tf, backend.tf, staging.tfvars)
│   └── prod/      (main.tf, backend.tf, prod.tfvars)
└── sim/src/main/java/com/bank/tfmod/
    ├── ModuleDemo.java        (runnable demo + main)
    ├── Account.java
    ├── Module.java            (reusable parameterized unit)
    ├── EnvironmentRoot.java   (composes modules + own state)
    └── BankLogFormatter.java
```

##### 4c. Terraform module and environment root

```hcl
# modules/eks/variables.tf — typed inputs with descriptions
variable "node_count"    { type = number, description = "worker node count" }
variable "instance_type" { type = string, description = "EC2 type for nodes" }
variable "subnet_ids"    { type = list(string) }

# modules/eks/main.tf — the reusable logic (same for all envs)
resource "aws_eks_node_group" "ng" {
  node_group_name = "bank-ng"
  subnet_ids      = var.subnet_ids
  instance_types  = [var.instance_type]
  scaling_config { desired_size = var.node_count, min_size = var.node_count, max_size = var.node_count }
}

# modules/eks/outputs.tf
output "node_group_name" { value = aws_eks_node_group.ng.node_group_name }
```

```hcl
# envs/prod/main.tf — thin root composes shared modules with PROD inputs
module "network" { source = "../../modules/network"  cidr = "10.0.0.0/16" }
module "eks" {
  source        = "../../modules/eks"
  node_count    = 10
  instance_type = "m5.2xlarge"
  subnet_ids    = module.network.subnet_ids   # wire module output -> input
}

# envs/prod/backend.tf — SEPARATE state key per environment (isolation)
terraform { backend "s3" {
  bucket = "nbi-terraform-state", key = "prod/terraform.tfstate",
  dynamodb_table = "nbi-terraform-locks", encrypt = true } }
```

```bash
cd ../staging   && terraform init && terraform apply -var-file=staging.tfvars
cd ../prod      && terraform init && terraform apply -var-file=prod.tfvars
# Lightweight variants via workspaces (e.g. per-developer sandboxes):
terraform workspace new feature-x && terraform workspace select feature-x
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: shared network and EKS modules, instantiated by three environment roots with different inputs.

Step 1 — The dev root declares its own state key and calls the network module with a dev CIDR, which outputs two dev subnet IDs. It then calls the EKS module with two t3.medium nodes, wiring the subnet IDs in, and produces a small dev node group. The dev state is isolated under its own key.

Step 2 — The staging root does the same with its own state key, a staging CIDR, and four m5.large nodes, producing a medium node group from the identical module code.

Step 3 — The production root declares its own state key, calls the network module with the production CIDR, and calls the EKS module with ten m5.2xlarge nodes, producing a large production node group. Because all three used the same module code, their structure is guaranteed consistent and cannot drift, while their inputs and state are fully separated.

Step 4 — The wiring of the network module's subnet outputs into the EKS module's inputs shows module composition: one module's results feed another, exactly as in real Terraform.

Step 5 — Because the production cluster was produced correctly from the shared module, a transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya runs on it successfully, connecting the module structure to a working banking operation.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Terraform module is a reusable, parameterized container of resources that I define once and instantiate many times with different inputs, which is what keeps infrastructure code from being copy-pasted and drifting. A module declares typed input variables, creates its resources, and exposes outputs, and the root configuration calls child modules and wires one module's outputs into another's inputs, for example feeding a network module's subnet IDs into an EKS module. Good modules do one coherent job, expose clear inputs and outputs, and are versioned when published, exactly like well-encapsulated functions.

A workspace is a named state copy of a single configuration within one backend, so the same configuration can manage several independent state files and I can branch behaviour on the workspace name. Workspaces are lightweight and genuinely useful for ephemeral or very similar variants like per-developer sandboxes or short-lived feature stacks. But I am careful with them for production, because all workspaces share the same backend and the same configuration code, and it is easy to run a command against the wrong workspace and hit production by accident, which is why in regulated banking I do not use workspaces to draw the production boundary.

For separating dev, staging, and production the structure I recommend is composition. I keep the reusable logic in a modules directory with modules like network, eks, and database, and I create a thin root per environment, each with its own backend state key, its own variable values, and module blocks that call the shared modules with environment-appropriate inputs. Production calls the EKS module with ten large nodes while dev calls it with two small nodes, all from the same module code. That gives strong isolation because each environment has its own locked, versioned state and its own blast radius, while the shared modules guarantee the environments stay structurally consistent.

In my project at the National Bank of India this came straight from pain. We used to copy the full configuration into three folders and they drifted, so staging and production diverged and a bug slipped past staging. Moving the logic into shared modules called from three thin roots eliminated the drift because all three environments now come from identical module code. And after someone nearly changed production by applying in the wrong workspace, we made the production boundary a separate root with its own isolated state rather than a workspace selection, so a mistake in a lower environment can never reach production. The result is reuse and consistency from modules, isolation and safety from per-environment roots, and workspaces reserved for the lightweight sandbox cases where they genuinely shine.

answers.question: What is configuration drift, how do you detect it (`terraform plan`), and how do you reconcile it?
answers.shortTitle: Configuration Drift: What It Is, How to Detect It, and How to Reconcile It

s1_definition.profdef: Configuration drift is the divergence between the real infrastructure and what the Terraform configuration and state describe, caused by changes made outside Terraform, such as a manual console edit, an automated process, or another tool. You detect it by running terraform plan, which refreshes the state against reality and shows any differences as proposed changes, or terraform plan with the refresh-only mode to see drift without proposing fixes. You reconcile it either by re-applying to push reality back to the declared configuration, by updating the configuration to adopt the out-of-band change deliberately, or by importing a resource that exists but is not yet tracked.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India the official blueprint and inventory ledger say the vault door has a specific lock. One night a technician manually swaps the lock without updating the ledger. Now the blueprint and the real vault disagree, which is drift. You find it by walking the branch with the ledger in hand and comparing, which is what plan does. You fix it either by restoring the lock the blueprint specifies, or by formally updating the blueprint to accept the new lock, or by adding a newly installed safe that nobody recorded into the ledger so future audits know about it.
s1_definition.oneliner: Drift is reality diverging from the declared configuration due to out-of-band changes; detect it with terraform plan and reconcile by re-applying, updating the config to match, or importing untracked resources.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Configuration drift is the divergence between the real infrastructure and what the Terraform configuration and state describe, caused by changes made outside Terraform, such as a manual console edit, an automated process, or another tool. You detect it by running terraform plan, which refreshes the state against reality and shows any differences as proposed changes, or terraform plan with the refresh-only mode to see drift without proposing fixes. You reconcile it either by re-applying to push reality back to the declared configuration, by updating the configuration to adopt the out-of-band change deliberately, or by importing a resource that exists but is not yet tracked.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India the official blueprint and inventory ledger say the vault door has a specific lock. One night a technician manually swaps the lock without updating the ledger. Now the blueprint and the real vault disagree, which is drift. You find it by walking the branch with the ledger in hand and comparing, which is what plan does. You fix it either by restoring the lock the blueprint specifies, or by formally updating the blueprint to accept the new lock, or by adding a newly installed safe that nobody recorded into the ledger so future audits know about it.

**One line to remember:** Drift is reality diverging from the declared configuration due to out-of-band changes; detect it with terraform plan and reconcile by re-applying, updating the config to match, or importing untracked resources.

sections.s2_technical:
Drift happens because Terraform is not the only actor that can change cloud resources. An engineer might open the AWS console and bump a database instance class during an incident, an auto-scaling process might change a setting, another team's tool might edit a security group, or a cloud provider might alter a default. Any of these makes the real resource differ from what Terraform's state and configuration say, and because Terraform plans by diffing desired configuration against state against reality, drift directly affects the next plan.

Detection starts with terraform plan. Plan first refreshes: it queries the providers for the current real attributes and compares them to the state. If reality differs from the configuration, plan shows changes that would bring reality back in line, which surfaces the drift as a set of proposed updates. To inspect drift without any intent to change, I use plan in refresh-only mode, which reports what changed in reality relative to state so I can decide deliberately, and I can also run a refresh-only apply to update the state to match reality without touching resources. In mature setups I run a scheduled plan in CI, often called drift detection, that alerts the team when the real world no longer matches the declared configuration, so drift is caught proactively rather than discovered during the next change.

Reconciliation has three distinct strategies and choosing correctly matters. The first is to re-apply the existing configuration, which pushes reality back to what the code declares, effectively reverting the manual change. This is the right choice when the out-of-band change was unintended or unauthorized, because the configuration is the source of truth and should win. The second is to update the configuration to match the new reality, which is the right choice when the manual change was actually desirable, for example an emergency scale-up during an incident that should be made permanent, so I codify it and apply so state and code agree. The third is terraform import, used when a resource exists in the cloud but is not in the state at all, which is a form of drift where Terraform is simply unaware of a resource; import brings it under management so future plans account for it. A refresh-only apply is a fourth, narrower tool to realign state with reality without changing either resources or configuration.

The senior discipline is preventive and procedural. I minimize drift by forbidding manual console changes to Terraform-managed resources, routing all changes through code and the pipeline, and using guardrails like IAM policies that restrict who can modify managed resources directly. I run scheduled drift detection so surprises are caught early. And when drift does occur, I make a conscious decision per resource whether the code should win or reality should win, rather than blindly applying, because in a bank blindly reverting an emergency fix or blindly adopting an unauthorized change can both be dangerous. Drift handling is as much about process and intent as it is about the plan command.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India our ledger database and security groups are Terraform-managed, and drift bit us in two instructive ways.

Problem 1 — during a late-night incident an on-call engineer manually bumped the ledger database instance class in the console to handle load and did not tell anyone. The next Terraform plan showed it wanted to shrink the database back, which would have hurt production. This is exactly the decision point: revert via re-apply, or adopt the change in code.

Problem 2 — another team created a security group rule directly in the console that Terraform did not know about, so it was untracked drift. The fix was to import it so it became managed. This is exactly the import scenario.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `CloudReality` holding actual resource attributes, a `TerraformState` holding the declared values, a `DriftDetector` that diffs them like terraform plan, and a `Reconciler` that applies one of the three strategies. We detect the database drift and the untracked security group, decide per resource, and then run a transfer for Rajesh and Priya on the correctly reconciled database.

Step 4 — Separately, a security group rule was created directly in the console. A plan finds it exists in the cloud but is not tracked by Terraform, flagging it as a candidate for import. We run import so the rule becomes managed and future plans account for it.

Step 5 — With the database class correctly reconciled and the rule now tracked, a transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya runs on the ledger database successfully, tying the reconciled infrastructure to a working operation.

answers.question: (Scenario) The Terraform state file is accidentally deleted, or `terraform apply` fails midway leaving partially-created resources — how do you recover (state backup/versioning, `terraform import`, targeted apply)?
answers.shortTitle: (Scenario) Terraform State Deleted or an Apply Fails Midway — How to Recover

s1_definition.profdef: These are two related disaster scenarios. If the state file is deleted, Terraform loses its map from configuration to real resources and will try to recreate everything, so recovery means restoring the state from a backup, typically S3 object versioning or a local backup, or if no backup exists, rebuilding the state with terraform import for each existing resource. If an apply fails midway, some resources were created and recorded while others were not, leaving a partial deployment; recovery means inspecting the state, re-running apply to continue from where it stopped, and using targeted apply or import to fix the specific resources that are inconsistent.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India the inventory ledger is how the bank knows which vault and ATMs it already owns. If the ledger is shredded, the bank might wrongly think it owns nothing and try to buy a second vault, so you restore the ledger from the head-office backup copy, or if there is no backup you physically walk the branch and re-enter each existing item into a fresh ledger. If a renovation is interrupted halfway, with the new counters installed but the ledger not yet updated, you compare what is physically there against the ledger and finish the job carefully, item by item, rather than restarting the whole renovation.
s1_definition.oneliner: Restore deleted state from S3 versioning or backup, or rebuild it with terraform import; for a half-finished apply, inspect state and re-run apply, using targeted apply and import to fix only the inconsistent resources.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** These are two related disaster scenarios. If the state file is deleted, Terraform loses its map from configuration to real resources and will try to recreate everything, so recovery means restoring the state from a backup, typically S3 object versioning or a local backup, or if no backup exists, rebuilding the state with terraform import for each existing resource. If an apply fails midway, some resources were created and recorded while others were not, leaving a partial deployment; recovery means inspecting the state, re-running apply to continue from where it stopped, and using targeted apply or import to fix the specific resources that are inconsistent.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India the inventory ledger is how the bank knows which vault and ATMs it already owns. If the ledger is shredded, the bank might wrongly think it owns nothing and try to buy a second vault, so you restore the ledger from the head-office backup copy, or if there is no backup you physically walk the branch and re-enter each existing item into a fresh ledger. If a renovation is interrupted halfway, with the new counters installed but the ledger not yet updated, you compare what is physically there against the ledger and finish the job carefully, item by item, rather than restarting the whole renovation.

**One line to remember:** Restore deleted state from S3 versioning or backup, or rebuild it with terraform import; for a half-finished apply, inspect state and re-run apply, using targeted apply and import to fix only the inconsistent resources.

sections.s2_technical:
The reason a deleted state is so dangerous is that the state is Terraform's only memory of what it created. Without it, Terraform compares the configuration against an empty state and concludes every resource must be created fresh, so the next apply would try to duplicate a production VPC, cluster, and database. The first and best recovery is to restore the state, which is exactly why remote state with S3 object versioning matters: every write creates a new object version, so a deleted or corrupted state can be restored by promoting a previous version. If you kept a local backup, Terraform also writes a terraform.tfstate.backup file on each apply that holds the prior state, which can rescue you locally.

If no backup exists at all, you rebuild the state by importing each real resource. terraform import takes a resource address from the configuration and the real cloud identifier and records the mapping into state without changing the resource. This is tedious because you import resources one by one and must know each real ID, but it fully reconstructs the state so Terraform stops wanting to recreate things. After importing, a plan should show no changes if the configuration matches reality.

A midway apply failure is different. Terraform applies resources in dependency order and records each success in state as it goes, so when apply fails partway, the resources created before the failure are real and tracked, while the failing resource and everything after it are not. Terraform usually reports exactly which resource failed and why. The primary recovery is simply to fix the cause, such as a quota limit, a bad input, or a transient API error, and run apply again; Terraform reads the state, sees what already exists, and continues from where it stopped rather than restarting. If the failing resource was left in a half-created, tainted condition, I can replace it on the next apply. If I want to proceed carefully and touch only specific resources, I use a targeted apply that limits the operation to a named resource or module, which is useful to repair one broken resource without risking the rest, though I treat targeting as a surgical tool rather than a normal workflow. If the failure created a real resource that never got recorded in state, that is untracked drift, and I use import to bring it under management so a retry does not duplicate it.

The senior discipline is prevention and calm procedure. I always use remote state with versioning and locking so a deletion is recoverable and concurrent applies cannot cause partial chaos, I never edit state by hand except as a last resort with the state commands, and I back up state before risky operations. When disaster strikes I resist the urge to run a blind apply, because an apply against a lost or inconsistent state can destroy or duplicate production resources. Instead I first restore or reconstruct the state, then run a plan to see exactly what Terraform intends, and only apply once the plan matches my understanding of reality. In a bank, that discipline is the difference between a quiet recovery and an outage.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India both halves of this scenario happened, which is why we drilled the recovery.

Problem 1 — a cleanup script accidentally deleted the state object. Because the S3 bucket had versioning on, we restored the previous version and a plan immediately showed no changes, confirming recovery. Without versioning we would have had to import the VPC, cluster, and database by hand.

Problem 2 — an apply that was adding a new read-replica database failed midway because of a quota limit, after the networking was created but before the replica. Re-running apply after raising the quota continued from where it stopped, and a targeted apply let us repair just the replica without touching the healthy resources.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `VersionedStateStore` that can be deleted and restored, a `StatefulApply` that records resources as it creates them and can fail midway, and a `Recovery` helper offering restore-from-version, import, and targeted apply. We delete the state and restore it, then fail an apply midway and recover, finally running a transfer for Rajesh and Priya on the recovered database.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a three-resource infrastructure, a state deletion, and a later expansion that fails midway.

Step 1 — The initial apply creates the VPC, cluster, and ledger database, recording each in state and saving a version. The state now knows all three resources exist.

Step 2 — Disaster one strikes: a script deletes the state object, so Terraform now believes nothing exists and would try to recreate everything, risking duplicate production resources.

Step 3 — Recovery restores the last good state version from S3 versioning. A follow-up apply reads the restored state, sees all three resources already present, and creates nothing, confirming a clean recovery with no duplicates. Had there been no backup, we would have imported each resource by real ID instead.

Step 4 — Disaster two strikes: an expansion applies a replica network and then a read-replica database, but the replica fails midway on a quota limit. The subnet was created and recorded, while the replica was not, leaving a partial state. The log shows the partial state containing the subnet but not the replica.

Step 5 — After raising the quota, a targeted apply repairs only the replica database without touching the healthy resources. With the infrastructure fully recovered, a transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya runs successfully on the ledger database.

sections.s6_takeaway:
These are two related disasters, and in both the single most important rule is to never run a blind apply, because an apply against a lost or inconsistent state can duplicate or destroy production resources. The state is Terraform's only memory of what it created, so I always recover or reconstruct the state first, run a plan to confirm what Terraform intends, and only apply once the plan matches reality.

If the state file is deleted, Terraform compares the configuration against an empty state and concludes it must create everything fresh, which in production means trying to build a second VPC, cluster, and database. The best recovery is to restore the state, which is exactly why I keep remote state in a versioned S3 bucket: every write is a new object version, so I promote the last good version and a follow-up plan should show no changes, confirming the restore matched reality. Locally, Terraform also writes a backup state file on each apply that can rescue me. If there is no backup at all, I rebuild the state with terraform import, taking each resource address and its real cloud identifier to record the mapping without changing the resource, which is tedious but fully reconstructs the state so Terraform stops wanting to recreate things.

If an apply fails midway, Terraform applies in dependency order and records each success as it goes, so the resources before the failure are real and tracked while the failing one and everything after it are not, leaving a partial deployment. The primary recovery is to fix the root cause, such as a quota limit or a bad input, and simply run apply again, because Terraform reads the state, sees what already exists, and continues from where it stopped rather than restarting. If I want to be surgical, I use a targeted apply to repair only the broken resource without risking the healthy ones, and if the failure created a real resource that never got recorded, I import it so a retry does not duplicate it.

In my project at the National Bank of India both happened. A cleanup script deleted the state object, but because the bucket had versioning on, we restored the previous version and a plan immediately showed no changes. And an expansion that added a read-replica failed midway on a quota limit after the networking was created, so once we raised the quota we re-ran apply to continue and used a targeted apply to repair just the replica without touching the healthy resources. The discipline I carry from that is that remote state with versioning and locking turns a potential outage into a calm, procedural recovery, and the order is always restore or rebuild the state, plan, then apply, never apply first.

answers.question: What is the difference between `terraform taint`/`-replace` and `terraform import`, and how do you reference one module's resources from another (outputs/remote state)?
answers.shortTitle: Terraform taint/-replace vs import, and Referencing One Module's Resources from Another

s1_definition.profdef: terraform taint, now superseded by the apply flag minus-replace, marks a resource that Terraform already manages for destruction and recreation on the next apply, used when a resource is unhealthy but its configuration is unchanged. terraform import does the opposite direction: it takes a resource that exists in the cloud but is not yet in Terraform's state and records it so Terraform starts managing it, without creating or destroying anything. To reference one module's resources from another within the same configuration you wire outputs from one module into the inputs of another, and across separately-applied configurations you read another configuration's outputs through the terraform_remote_state data source.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the replace action is like telling maintenance to rip out a specific faulty ATM you already own and install a fresh one in its place, even though the blueprint for that ATM did not change. Import is the reverse: an ATM was installed by a contractor and never entered into the inventory ledger, so you add it to the ledger so the bank officially manages it from now on, without touching the machine. Referencing between modules is like the vault module publishing the vault's location so the security-camera module can point a camera at it, either by handing over the address directly within one project or by looking it up from another department's published records.
s1_definition.oneliner: replace destroys-and-recreates a managed resource, import adopts an unmanaged one into state, and modules share data by wiring outputs into inputs or reading terraform_remote_state across configurations.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** terraform taint, now superseded by the apply flag minus-replace, marks a resource that Terraform already manages for destruction and recreation on the next apply, used when a resource is unhealthy but its configuration is unchanged. terraform import does the opposite direction: it takes a resource that exists in the cloud but is not yet in Terraform's state and records it so Terraform starts managing it, without creating or destroying anything. To reference one module's resources from another within the same configuration you wire outputs from one module into the inputs of another, and across separately-applied configurations you read another configuration's outputs through the terraform_remote_state data source.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, the replace action is like telling maintenance to rip out a specific faulty ATM you already own and install a fresh one in its place, even though the blueprint for that ATM did not change. Import is the reverse: an ATM was installed by a contractor and never entered into the inventory ledger, so you add it to the ledger so the bank officially manages it from now on, without touching the machine. Referencing between modules is like the vault module publishing the vault's location so the security-camera module can point a camera at it, either by handing over the address directly within one project or by looking it up from another department's published records.

**One line to remember:** replace destroys-and-recreates a managed resource, import adopts an unmanaged one into state, and modules share data by wiring outputs into inputs or reading terraform_remote_state across configurations.

sections.s2_technical:
The replace operation addresses a resource Terraform already knows about but that has gone bad in a way the configuration cannot express. Maybe a virtual machine is in a corrupted state, a certificate on a resource needs regenerating, or a managed instance is misbehaving, yet the declared configuration is correct and unchanged. In that case I want Terraform to destroy that specific resource and create a fresh one. The old way was terraform taint, which marked the resource in state so the next apply would replace it, and the corresponding terraform untaint reversed the mark. The modern and preferred way is to skip the separate marking step and run apply or plan with the minus-replace flag naming the resource address, which shows the destroy-and-recreate in the plan so I can review it before applying. The key point is that replace operates entirely on a resource that is already under management; it changes nothing about ownership, only forces a recreate.

import solves the opposite problem: a resource exists in the real cloud but Terraform has no record of it in state, so Terraform would either ignore it or, worse, try to create a duplicate. This happens when a resource was created manually, by another tool, or when rebuilding a lost state. terraform import takes the resource address as written in the configuration and the real provider-specific identifier, and writes the mapping into state so Terraform now manages that existing resource. Import never creates or destroys anything; it only adopts. After an import I run a plan and expect no changes if my configuration accurately describes the imported resource, and if the plan wants changes I reconcile the configuration to match. So replace and import move in opposite directions: replace takes a managed resource and recreates it, while import takes an unmanaged resource and starts managing it.

Referencing resources between modules is about passing data cleanly rather than reaching into another module's internals. Within a single configuration, a child module declares output values exposing exactly what callers may use, such as a VPC module outputting its subnet IDs. The root or another module then reads that with the module dot name dot output syntax and passes it as an input variable to the consuming module, for example feeding the network module's subnet IDs into the EKS module's subnet input. This keeps modules encapsulated: a module exposes a deliberate contract of outputs and never lets callers depend on its internal resource names.

Across separately-applied configurations, where the networking stack and the application stack are applied independently with their own state files, you cannot use the module reference syntax because the resources live in a different state. Instead the producing configuration declares outputs, and the consuming configuration reads them with the terraform_remote_state data source, which points at the producer's backend such as its S3 state key and exposes its outputs. The consumer then uses those values, for example reading the shared VPC's subnet IDs from the networking state. The senior discipline is to prefer explicit outputs and, where possible, provider data sources or published parameters over tightly coupling two states, because terraform_remote_state creates a hard dependency on another configuration's internal state layout, and in a large bank platform I often expose shared values through a more stable contract like SSM parameters that the consumer reads with a normal data source, decoupling the stacks. The through-line is that modules and configurations communicate through declared outputs, never by reaching into each other's resources directly.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India these three tools each solved a real problem on our platform.

Problem 1 — a managed NAT gateway got into a bad state that the configuration could not fix, so we needed to force a recreate of just that one resource without changing anything else. This is exactly the minus-replace use case.

Problem 2 — a contractor created an S3 audit bucket manually and we needed Terraform to manage it going forward without recreating it and losing the audit logs. This is exactly the import use case.

Problem 3 — our networking stack and application stack are applied separately, and the application's EKS module needs the shared VPC's subnet IDs, which live in the networking stack's state. This is exactly the terraform_remote_state and output use case.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `ManagedResource` that can be marked for replace, an `ImportTool` that adopts an unmanaged resource, a `ModuleOutputs` registry for in-configuration wiring, and a `RemoteStateReader` for cross-stack references. We replace the NAT gateway, import the audit bucket, wire subnet outputs into EKS, and run a transfer for Rajesh and Priya on the resulting cluster.

```
tf-ops/

├── application/ (reads terraform_remote_state of networking)

│   ├── Account.java
│   ├── ManagedResource.java    (replace = destroy+recreate)
│   ├── ImportTool.java         (adopt unmanaged into state)
│   ├── ModuleOutputs.java      (in-config output→input wiring)
│   ├── RemoteStateReader.java  (cross-stack outputs)
│   └── BankLogFormatter.java
```

##### 4c. Terraform outputs and remote state reference

```hcl
# networking/outputs.tf — the producing stack publishes a contract
output "subnet_ids" { value = aws_subnet.private[*].id }
output "vpc_id"     { value = aws_vpc.bank.id }

# application/main.tf — consuming stack reads the networking stack's outputs
data "terraform_remote_state" "networking" {
  backend = "s3"
  config = {
    bucket = "nbi-terraform-state"
    key    = "networking/terraform.tfstate"   # producer's state key
    region = "ap-south-1"
  }
}
module "eks" {
  source     = "../modules/eks"
  subnet_ids = data.terraform_remote_state.networking.outputs.subnet_ids  # cross-stack ref
}
```

```bash
# Real Terraform

terraform apply -replace=aws_nat_gateway.bank      # modern replacement for `terraform taint`
terraform import aws_s3_bucket.audit nbi-audit-logs # adopt an existing bucket into state
terraform plan                                      # expect NO changes after a correct import
# cross-stack reference uses data "terraform_remote_state" in the consuming config
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: an unhealthy managed NAT gateway, an unmanaged audit bucket, and two stacks that must share subnet IDs.

Step 1 — The NAT gateway is already managed with a real ID. We mark it for replacement because it is in a bad state the configuration cannot fix. On apply, Terraform destroys the old NAT and creates a fresh one with a new ID, while nothing else changes. This is the replace direction: recreate a managed resource.

Step 2 — The audit bucket exists in the cloud but Terraform does not track it. The import tool adopts it into state using its real name, so Terraform now manages it without recreating it, which preserves the existing audit logs. This is the opposite direction: adopt an unmanaged resource.

Step 3 — Within one configuration, the networking module publishes its subnet IDs as an output. The EKS module reads that output and uses it as its subnet input, demonstrating clean in-configuration wiring through a declared contract rather than reaching into the networking module's internals.

Step 4 — Across separately-applied stacks, the networking stack publishes its outputs to its own state. The application stack reads those outputs through the remote-state reader keyed by the networking stack's state, retrieving the production subnet IDs without sharing a single state file.

Step 5 — The production EKS cluster is built on the subnets obtained from remote state, and a transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya runs on it successfully, tying all three tools to a working banking operation.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The replace operation and import move in opposite directions, and keeping that straight is the heart of the answer. Replace, which used to be done with terraform taint and is now done with the apply minus-replace flag, takes a resource Terraform already manages and forces it to be destroyed and recreated on the next apply. I reach for it when a resource is unhealthy in a way the configuration cannot express, such as a corrupted virtual machine or a NAT gateway stuck in a bad state, while the declared configuration itself is correct and unchanged. The modern minus-replace flag is better than the old taint command because it shows the destroy-and-recreate in the plan so I review it before applying, and crucially it changes nothing about ownership, it only forces a recreate.

Import does the reverse. It takes a resource that exists in the real cloud but is not in Terraform's state, and records the mapping so Terraform starts managing it, without creating or destroying anything. I use it when a resource was created manually or by another tool, or when rebuilding a lost state. After an import I always run a plan and expect no changes, and if the plan wants changes I adjust the configuration to match the imported reality. So replace recreates a managed resource while import adopts an unmanaged one, and confusing the two can either needlessly destroy a healthy resource or accidentally duplicate an existing one.

Referencing resources between modules is about passing data through declared contracts rather than reaching into internals. Within one configuration, a module exposes output values, and the caller reads them with the module dot name dot output syntax and passes them as inputs to another module, for example feeding a network module's subnet IDs into an EKS module. Across separately-applied configurations with their own state files, I cannot use that syntax because the resources live in a different state, so the producer declares outputs and the consumer reads them through the terraform_remote_state data source pointed at the producer's backend. In a large platform I often go one step further and publish shared values through a more stable contract like SSM parameters that the consumer reads with a normal data source, because that decouples the stacks instead of hard-wiring one configuration to another's internal state layout.

In my project at the National Bank of India all three showed up. A managed NAT gateway went bad and we used minus-replace to recreate just that one resource without disturbing anything else. A contractor created an audit bucket manually and we imported it so Terraform managed it going forward without recreating it and losing the logs. And because our networking and application stacks are applied separately, the application's EKS module reads the shared VPC's subnet IDs from the networking stack through remote state outputs. The unifying principle I always state is that modules and configurations communicate through deliberately declared outputs, never by reaching into each other's resources, and that replace and import are precise, opposite tools that I apply consciously rather than interchangeably.

answers.question: How do you bring existing (manually-created or legacy) AWS resources under Terraform management as a workflow — write the matching resource config → `terraform import` into state → `terraform plan` → iterate on the config until the plan proposes NO unexpected changes → commit — and why does importing into state NOT automatically produce correct/clean config (you still must author accurate HCL, strip noise, introduce variables/modules)?
answers.shortTitle: Bringing existing/legacy AWS resources under Terraform management (write config → import → plan → iterate → commit), and why import alone does not produce clean config

s1_definition.profdef: `terraform import` binds an already-existing real-world infrastructure object to a Terraform resource address in the state file. It populates state only; it does not generate configuration. The correct adoption workflow is to first author HCL that matches the live resource, run `terraform import` to map the real object into state, run `terraform plan`, and then iterate on the HCL until the plan shows no changes, because a clean plan proves that your configuration and the real resource are in agreement.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has an old safe-deposit vault that a contractor installed years ago without any paperwork. Terraform is the bank's official asset register. Importing is like writing the vault's serial number into the register so the bank now "knows" it owns the vault. But writing the serial number does NOT describe the vault — its size, lock type, and location. You still have to walk to the vault, measure it, and write an accurate description by hand. If your written description says "small vault" but the real vault is large, the next audit (the plan) will scream "mismatch." You keep fixing your description until the audit is silent.
s1_definition.oneliner: Import fills state, not config — you still hand-write accurate HCL until `terraform plan` shows zero drift.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `terraform import` binds an already-existing real-world infrastructure object to a Terraform resource address in the state file. It populates state only; it does not generate configuration. The correct adoption workflow is to first author HCL that matches the live resource, run `terraform import` to map the real object into state, run `terraform plan`, and then iterate on the HCL until the plan shows no changes, because a clean plan proves that your configuration and the real resource are in agreement.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has an old safe-deposit vault that a contractor installed years ago without any paperwork. Terraform is the bank's official asset register. Importing is like writing the vault's serial number into the register so the bank now "knows" it owns the vault. But writing the serial number does NOT describe the vault — its size, lock type, and location. You still have to walk to the vault, measure it, and write an accurate description by hand. If your written description says "small vault" but the real vault is large, the next audit (the plan) will scream "mismatch." You keep fixing your description until the audit is silent.

**One line to remember:** Import fills state, not config — you still hand-write accurate HCL until `terraform plan` shows zero drift.

sections.s2_technical:
Terraform tracks three things: the configuration (your HCL files, the desired state), the state file (Terraform's record of what it manages), and the real infrastructure (what actually exists in AWS). A normal `terraform apply` keeps all three in sync. When a resource was created manually outside Terraform, the state file knows nothing about it, so Terraform would try to CREATE a duplicate if you naively wrote config and applied. Import solves exactly this: it writes a state entry that says "this Terraform address corresponds to this real AWS object."

The classic command form is `terraform import aws_s3_bucket.audit nbi-audit-logs-prod`, where `aws_s3_bucket.audit` is the resource address you must have already declared in HCL (even if it is an empty shell), and `nbi-audit-logs-prod` is the real bucket name AWS uses as its import ID. Each resource type documents its own import ID format — a bucket uses its name, an EC2 instance uses `i-0abc123`, a security group uses `sg-0abc123`, a route table association uses a compound ID.

Here is why import alone is never enough. Import reads the live attributes into state, but your HCL is still whatever you typed. If your HCL omits `versioning`, `server_side_encryption_configuration`, or `tags` that the real bucket has, the first plan will propose to REMOVE or CHANGE them, because Terraform believes your config is the desired truth. So you run `terraform plan`, read every single proposed change, and copy the real settings into your HCL until the plan is empty. This is the iterate loop. Newer Terraform (1.5+) adds an `import {}` block and `terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf` which can scaffold HCL for you, but the generated HCL is noisy — it dumps every computed and default attribute — so you still must strip read-only fields, replace hardcoded values with `var.` references, and group resources into modules.

A senior nuance: never import straight into production state on your first attempt. Take a backup of the state (`terraform state pull > backup.tfstate`), import, and if the plan looks wrong you can `terraform state rm` the address to undo the mapping without touching the real resource. Import only edits state; it never mutates AWS.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India, a security contractor manually created an S3 bucket called `nbi-audit-logs-prod` two years ago to store transaction audit logs for Rajesh's savings account SAV2001 and Priya's current account CUR3001. It has versioning on, AES-256 encryption, and a `team=compliance` tag. Nobody wrote Terraform for it. Now the platform team wants ALL infrastructure under Terraform so changes go through pull requests.

Problem 1 — The bucket exists but Terraform does not know about it. If an engineer writes `resource "aws_s3_bucket"` and runs apply, Terraform tries to CREATE a second bucket and fails because the name is globally taken, or worse, it would recreate and wipe audit history. This is exactly what import solves: we map the real bucket into state first.

Problem 2 — After import, the first plan wrongly wants to turn OFF versioning and encryption, because the engineer's HCL did not mention them. This is the "import does not write config" lesson. We must read the plan and hand-author the versioning and encryption blocks until the plan is clean.

Problem 3 — The raw config has the bucket name and region hardcoded. For reuse across environments we introduce variables. This is the "strip noise, introduce variables" step.

Our runnable Java simulation models this whole workflow as an in-memory engine: a `TerraformState` (what Terraform thinks it manages), a `LiveInfrastructure` (what AWS really has), and a `ConfiguredResource` (the HCL the engineer wrote). The `ImportEngine` has `importResource()` which copies the live ID into state WITHOUT copying attributes into config, and `plan()` which diffs config against live and reports proposed changes. We will see the plan complain, then we patch the config, then the plan goes clean.

The classes are: `LiveInfrastructure` (the real AWS bucket), `TerraformState` (managed addresses), `ConfiguredResource` (engineer's HCL), `ImportEngine` with `importResource()` and `plan()`, and a `TerraformImportDemo` main that runs the full import-plan-iterate loop and logs every step.
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build the Java simulation
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the import workflow demo
java -cp target/classes com.bank.iac.TerraformImportDemo

# The real Terraform workflow this simulates:
cd terraform
terraform init
# Terraform 1.5+ generates a starting config from the import block:
terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf
# Review generated.tf, strip computed/noise attrs, move values into variables.tf
terraform plan      # iterate until this shows: "No changes."
terraform apply     # applies the import, adopting the bucket into state
git add main.tf variables.tf && git commit -m "Adopt legacy audit bucket into Terraform"
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a real S3 bucket `nbi-audit-logs-prod` with versioning Enabled, AES256 encryption, and tag team=compliance, plus an engineer who writes minimal HCL that only mentions the bucket name and the team tag.

Step 1: The engineer authors a minimal `aws_s3_bucket.audit` block. At this point the config exists on disk but Terraform state has no entry for it, so a naive apply would try to create a duplicate.

Step 2: The engineer runs import, which binds the address `aws_s3_bucket.audit` to the live ID `nbi-audit-logs-prod` inside the state file. The config on disk is untouched — import wrote to state only, nothing else changed.

Step 3: The first plan compares the engineer's config against the live bucket. Because the config never mentioned versioning or encryption, Terraform believes those should be absent and proposes to remove them. The plan is dirty with two unexpected changes. The data that changed is the engineer's understanding; the real bucket and the state are stable.

Step 4: The engineer reads the plan and adds the versioning Enabled block and the AES256 encryption block to the HCL. The config on disk now matches reality.

Step 5: The second plan compares again and finds no differences. The plan is clean. Only now is it safe to commit the HCL to version control, because a clean plan proves config, state, and reality all agree.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Bringing an existing or legacy AWS resource under Terraform management is a deliberate four-step workflow, and the single most important thing to understand is that importing only edits Terraform's state file — it never writes your configuration for you. First I author HCL that I believe matches the live resource. Second I run terraform import, which binds my resource address to the real object's import ID inside state, so Terraform stops trying to create a duplicate. Third I run terraform plan and read every proposed change line by line. Fourth I iterate on my HCL, copying the real settings the plan is complaining about, until the plan reports no changes, and only then do I commit.

The reason import does not produce clean config is that import is a one-way read into state; it has no opinion about how your HCL should look. Even the newer generate-config-out feature, which does scaffold HCL, produces noisy output full of computed and default attributes that I still have to strip, and I still have to replace hardcoded values with variables and group resources into modules so the config is reusable and reviewable.

In my project at the National Bank of India, a contractor had manually created an S3 bucket called nbi-audit-logs-prod that stored transaction audit logs for accounts like Rajesh's SAV2001 and Priya's CUR3001, complete with versioning and AES-256 encryption. I wrote a minimal resource block, imported the bucket into state, and the very first plan tried to strip versioning and encryption because my config had not mentioned them. I read that plan, added the versioning and encryption blocks, moved the bucket name into a variable, and iterated until the plan was silent. Only a clean plan proves that my configuration, Terraform's state, and the real infrastructure all agree, and that is the exact moment adoption is safe to commit. The discipline I always emphasise is that a clean plan — not a successful import — is the finish line.
